title: 1.1 Sources and conventions
text: We begin with the common language of geometric measure theory: measures record size, rectifiable sets supply tangent planes, and currents and varifolds encode different geometric data. The Stack Project of Geometric Measure Theory and Variational Problems develops this language together with minimal surfaces, CMC surfaces, min-max theory, phase transitions, obstacle problems, and mean curvature flow. The exposition and elementary proofs are written for this project. Theorems used without proof are explicitly identified below; their cited proofs remain external dependencies. Remark 1.1.1 (The source editions) . 912105D5B712 The initial foundational corpus contains five distinct works or editions. Federer, Geometric Measure Theory (1969), supplies the systematic reference [ Fed69 ] . Simon's Introduction to Geometric Measure Theory , copyright 2017, 2018, is the main source for the initial statements [ Sim18 ] . The supplied 2014 version [ Sim14 ] is retained as a separate edition: its printed page numbers differ from those of the later text. White's Topics in GMT , with notes by Otis Chodosh dated November 6, 2014, supplies the flat-chain viewpoint [ WhiCho14 ] . The two supplied filenames for these notes are byte-for-byte identical and represent one bibliographic source. Fleming's 2016 article [ Fle16 ] supplies historical context for finite perimeter and integral currents. It is not used as a substitute for a detailed proof of the structure or compactness theorems. Source citations use the printed page numbers of these editions, not PDF viewer page numbers. In the two Simon files, a PDF page usually contains a two-page spread. The source inventory records file hashes and the page conventions so later additions can use the same editions. Remark 1.1.2 (Notation and prerequisites) . 4EDA6AEDEA07 Unless stated otherwise, $U$ is an open subset of $\mathbb {R}^ n$, $1\leq m\leq n$, and $B_ r(x)$ is the open Euclidean ball. We write $\mathcal{L}^ n$ for Lebesgue measure, $\omega _ m=\mathcal{L}^ m(B_1(0))$, and $\mu \llcorner E$ for the restriction of a measure to a measurable set $E$. The notation $W\Subset U$ means that $\overline W$ is compact and contained in $U$. Continuous compactly supported functions form $C_ c(U)$. We assume elementary Lebesgue integration, the dominated and monotone convergence theorems, and basic differential forms. These prerequisites have not yet been developed in the stack. All almost-everywhere statements specify their measure. Sets of finite perimeter are considered modulo $\mathcal{L}^ n$-null sets. Our normal to a set of finite perimeter points outward; Simon uses the inward normal in Chapter 3, Section 4. For currents we use the comass convention for mass, as explained in Definition 5.1.3 . Remark 1.1.3 (The expanded variational reference) . 57833B199F67 The first variational additions connect Pitts' book [ Pitts81 ] to minimal hypersurfaces and stability, cycle-space min-max theory, the volume spectrum, Morse index, Willmore geometry, CMC hypersurfaces, curvature networks, and Allen–Cahn theory. They draw on the sixteen additional supplied files, with editions and roles recorded in the source inventory. Those first two batches contained twenty-one distinct works or editions in twenty-two supplied files. The later library expansion adds checked passages on compactness, geometric inequalities, multiplicity, abundance, and flow singularities, together with a larger catalogue of sources awaiting detailed study. The History chapter connects these developments to their original problems and to first-person recollections. The current foundations include BV compactness, current operations and slicing, and the Plateau existence argument in Theorem 5.4.7 . The minimal-surface chapters now connect stability to scalar curvature, the two-dimensional Bernstein theorem, and the spectral criterion for cones. The CMC chapter distinguishes total-volume constraints from unrestricted area-minus-volume stability. The mean-curvature-flow chapter develops evolution equations, comparison, Gaussian monotonicity, entropy, rescaling, and the Brakke formulation in Definition 14.6.1 . The obstacle chapter still contains a model formulation and a variational inequality; level-set flows, finer singularity theory, free-boundary surfaces, and capillarity require further development. A cited theorem without a local proof remains an external dependency; a chapter in the table of contents does not mean that its subject is complete.

title: 2.1 Radon measures
text: Weak convergence is useful because geometric limits need not remain smooth. We first specify the measures and the topology used in the later chapters. The reference is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Sections 1 and 5. Definition 2.1.1 (Radon measure) . 5B8B37A79F3A A nonnegative Borel measure $\mu $ on an open set $U\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$ is a Radon measure if it is finite on compact subsets of $U$ and, for every Borel set $A\subset U$, \[  \mu (A)=\inf \{ \mu (O):A\subset O\subset U,\  O\text{ open}\}  =\sup \{ \mu (K):K\subset A,\  K\text{ compact}\} .  \] We use its completion when integrating measurable functions. Its support consists of the points $x\in U$ for which every neighborhood has positive measure. Local finiteness does not require $\mu (U)<\infty $. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Section 5, Definition 5.6, p. 31, for the corresponding outer-measure formulation. Definition 2.1.2 (Weak convergence of measures) . D58956DB1AAB Radon measures $\mu _ j$ converge weakly in $U$ to a Radon measure $\mu $, written $\mu _ j\rightharpoonup \mu $, if \[  \lim _{j\to \infty }\int _ U\varphi \, d\mu _ j=\int _ U\varphi \, d\mu \qquad \text{for every }\varphi \in C_ c(U).  \] This is also called vague convergence. Testing only compactly supported functions allows mass to escape toward infinity or the boundary of $U$. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Section 5. Theorem 2.1.3 (Local compactness of Radon measures) . EC3F5C88A198 Let $\mu _ j$ be nonnegative Radon measures on $U$ and suppose that \[  \sup _ j\mu _ j(K)<\infty \qquad \text{for every compact }K\subset U.  \] There are a subsequence $\mu _{j_ k}$ and a Radon measure $\mu $ on $U$ such that $\mu _{j_ k}\rightharpoonup \mu $ in $U$. Cited theorem; proof to be added. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Section 5, Theorem 5.15, pp. 38–39. The construction uses a diagonal subsequence on compact subsets and the Riesz representation theorem, Theorem 5.12 in that section. Proposition 2.1.4 (Lower semicontinuity on open sets) . E6E21F29D7CA If $\mu _ j\rightharpoonup \mu $ in $U$, then \[  \mu (O)\leq \liminf _{j\to \infty }\mu _ j(O) \qquad \text{for every open }O\subset U.  \] This is the open-set inequality accompanying weak convergence in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Section 5. Proof Fix $0\leq \varphi \leq 1$ with $\varphi \in C_ c(O)$. Weak convergence gives \[  \int \varphi \, d\mu =\lim _ j\int \varphi \, d\mu _ j\leq \liminf _ j\mu _ j(O).  \] For every compact $K\subset O$ we can choose such a function with $\varphi =1$ on $K$. Taking the supremum over $K$ and using inner regularity proves the assertion, including the case $\mu (O)=\infty $. $\square$

title: 2.2 Hausdorff measure and density
text: Hausdorff measure gives a notion of $m$-dimensional size before any tangent plane is known. We use the normalization in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Section 2. Definition 2.2.1 (Normalized Hausdorff measure) . 04D5BCC54A0E Let $m\geq 1$ be an integer and $A\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$. For $\delta >0$ define \[  \mathcal{H}^ m_\delta (A)=\inf \left\{  \sum _{i=1}^{\infty }\omega _ m\left(\frac{\operatorname {diam}E_ i}{2}\right)^ m: A\subset \bigcup _ iE_ i,\quad \operatorname {diam}E_ i<\delta \right\} , \qquad \mathcal{H}^ m(A)=\lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}\mathcal{H}^ m_\delta (A).  \] The empty cover gives value zero for $A=\varnothing $. The limit exists in $[0,\infty ]$ by monotonicity as $\delta $ decreases. We set $\mathcal{H}^0$ equal to counting measure. These are Borel regular outer measures. With this normalization $\mathcal{H}^ m=\mathcal{L}^ m$ on $\mathbb {R}^ m$; that identification is a cited result, not part of the definition. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, equations (2.1)–(2.5) and Theorem 2.6, pp. 11–14, and [ Fed69 ] , Section 2.10.2(1), p. 171. Proposition 2.2.2 (Lipschitz distortion of Hausdorff measure) . 2921BEDC2A31 Let $A\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$, let $f:A\to \mathbb {R}^ q$ be $L$-Lipschitz with $0<L<\infty $, and let $m\geq 1$. Then \[  \mathcal{H}^ m(f(A))\leq L^ m\mathcal{H}^ m(A).  \] In particular, Lipschitz maps take $\mathcal{H}^ m$-null sets to $\mathcal{H}^ m$-null sets. A constant map also has this null-set property. This follows directly from the covering definition in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Section 2. Proof Intersect each set in a $\delta $-cover of $A$ with $A$ and take its image under $f$. The image diameters are at most $L$ times the original diameters. Thus \[  \mathcal{H}^ m_{L\delta }(f(A))\leq L^ m\mathcal{H}^ m_\delta (A).  \] Let $\delta \downarrow 0$. For a constant map the image is empty or a singleton, whose $\mathcal{H}^ m$ measure is zero when $m\geq 1$. $\square$ Definition 2.2.3 (Density) . B88FEB8AC934 For a Radon measure $\mu $ on $U$, a point $x\in U$, and $m\geq 1$, define \[  \Theta ^{*m}(\mu ,x)=\limsup _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{\mu (B_ r(x))}{\omega _ m r^ m}, \qquad \Theta _*^ m(\mu ,x)=\liminf _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{\mu (B_ r(x))}{\omega _ m r^ m}.  \] When these agree, their common value is the density $\Theta ^ m(\mu ,x)$. The values may be infinite. For $\mu =\mathcal{H}^ m\llcorner M$ we also write $\Theta ^ m(M,x)$. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Section 3, p. 14. Example 2.2.4 (A plane with multiplicity) . F2FA6522C7DE Let $P$ be an affine $m$-plane, let $\theta >0$, and set $\mu =\theta \mathcal{H}^ m\llcorner P$. For every $x\in P$ and $r>0$, \[  \mu (B_ r(x))=\theta \omega _ mr^ m,\qquad \Theta ^ m(\mu ,x)=\theta .  \] Indeed, a Euclidean isometry identifies $P\cap B_ r(x)$ with an $m$-dimensional ball, and the normalized Hausdorff measure agrees with Lebesgue measure on that plane. This model fixes the normalization used for tangent planes and varifolds below.

title: 3.1 Rectifiable sets and tangent planes
text: Lipschitz parametrizations are differentiable almost everywhere. Their images therefore provide the basic class of sets on which tangent-plane geometry survives. We follow [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Section 1, and Chapter 3, Section 1. Definition 3.1.1 (Countable rectifiability) . F69B7B515F3F An $\mathcal{H}^ m$-measurable set $M\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$ is countably $m$-rectifiable if there are Lipschitz maps $f_ i:\mathbb {R}^ m\to \mathbb {R}^ n$ such that \[  \mathcal{H}^ m\left(M\setminus \bigcup _{i=1}^{\infty }f_ i(\mathbb {R}^ m)\right)=0.  \] Local finiteness of $\mathcal{H}^ m\llcorner M$ is an additional hypothesis when needed, not part of this definition. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Definition 1.1, p. 85; compare [ WhiCho14 ] , Section 7, pp. 33–34. In Federer's notation this is countable $(\mathcal{H}^ m,m)$ rectifiability; his “countably $m$ rectifiable” requires an exact countable union. See [ Fed69 ] , Section 3.2.14, pp. 251–252. The null exceptional set must be retained when translating between the conventions. Theorem 3.1.2 (Rademacher) . 27C55CB3CC94 Let $V\subset \mathbb {R}^ m$ be open and let $f:V\to \mathbb {R}^ n$ be locally Lipschitz. Then for $\mathcal{L}^ m$-almost every $x\in V$ there is a linear map $Df(x):\mathbb {R}^ m\to \mathbb {R}^ n$ such that \[  \lim _{h\to 0}\frac{|f(x+h)-f(x)-Df(x)h|}{|h|}=0.  \] Cited theorem; proof to be added. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 1.4, pp. 44–46, for the scalar theorem. The displayed form follows by applying that theorem to each coordinate and localizing to balls compactly contained in $V$. Definition 3.1.3 (Approximate tangent plane) . 455A7C72F775 Let $M\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$ be $\mathcal{H}^ m$-measurable with locally finite $\mathcal{H}^ m$ measure. An $m$-dimensional linear subspace $P$ is the approximate tangent plane to $M$ at $x$ if \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}r^{-m}\int _ M\varphi \left(\frac{y-x}{r}\right)\, d\mathcal{H}^ m(y) =\int _ P\varphi \, d\mathcal{H}^ m \quad \text{for every }\varphi \in C_ c(\mathbb {R}^ n).  \] When it exists, it is unique and is denoted by $T_ xM$. This is the measure-limit convention in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Definition 1.4, pp. 86–87; it includes unit density. Uniqueness follows because the limiting measures have supports equal to their respective planes. Theorem 3.1.4 (Tangent planes on rectifiable sets) . 07FB5BA849C0 Let $M\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$ be $\mathcal{H}^ m$-measurable and satisfy $\mathcal{H}^ m(M\cap K)<\infty $ for every compact $K$. Then $M$ is countably $m$-rectifiable if and only if $T_ xM$ in Definition 3.1.3 exists at $\mathcal{H}^ m$-almost every $x\in M$. In particular, a countably $m$-rectifiable set with this local finiteness property satisfies \[  \Theta ^ m(\mathcal{H}^ m\llcorner M,x)=1 \quad \text{for }\mathcal{H}^ m\text{-almost every }x\in M.  \] Cited theorem; proof to be added. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 1.6 and Remark 1.5(3), p. 87. The density conclusion follows from the tangent-measure limit by approximating the indicator of the unit ball with continuous test functions. Local finiteness is essential to this formulation.

title: 3.2 Area and coarea
text: The area formula counts points in the fibers of a parametrization. The coarea formula integrates the measures of higher-dimensional fibers. We state Euclidean versions first, with different Jacobians made explicit. Definition 3.2.1 (Area and coarea Jacobians) . ECFDA4F8C960 For a linear map $L:\mathbb {R}^ m\to \mathbb {R}^ n$ with $m\leq n$, define its area Jacobian by \[  J_ mL=\sqrt{\det (L^*L)}.  \] For $L:\mathbb {R}^ n\to \mathbb {R}^ m$ with $m\leq n$, define its coarea Jacobian by \[  J_ mL=\sqrt{\det (LL^*)}.  \] Here $L^*$ is the Euclidean adjoint. Each quantity is zero when $L$ has rank less than $m$. For a locally Lipschitz map, use the appropriate expression with $L=Df(x)$ at points of differentiability, and set it to zero on the exceptional null set. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, equation (3.2), p. 57, and Chapter 3, equation (2.7), p. 93. Theorem 3.2.2 (Area formula) . 893CBC15202C Let $V\subset \mathbb {R}^ m$ be open, let $m\leq n$, let $f:V\to \mathbb {R}^ n$ be locally Lipschitz, and let $A\subset V$ be Lebesgue measurable. Then the multiplicity function on the right is $\mathcal{H}^ m$-measurable and \[  \int _ A J_ mDf(x)\, d\mathcal{L}^ m(x) =\int _{\mathbb {R}^ n}\mathcal{H}^0\bigl (A\cap f^{-1}(\{ y\} )\bigr )\, d\mathcal{H}^ m(y).  \] Both sides may be infinite. If $f$ is injective on $A$, the right side is $\mathcal{H}^ m(f(A))$. Cited theorem; proof to be added. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 3.3, p. 57. See also [ Fed69 ] , Theorem 3.2.3, p. 243. Rademacher's theorem supplies the derivative; the area formula is a further theorem and does not follow from differentiability alone. Corollary 3.2.3 (Area of a scalar graph) . C022A573234B Let $V\subset \mathbb {R}^ m$ be open, let $u:V\to \mathbb {R}$ be locally Lipschitz, and let $A\subset V$ be Lebesgue measurable. Then \[  \mathcal{H}^ m\{ (x,u(x)):x\in A\}  =\int _ A\sqrt{1+|Du(x)|^2}\, d\mathcal{L}^ m(x).  \] Proof The map $F(x)=(x,u(x))$ is locally Lipschitz and injective. At almost every point, $(DF)^*DF=I+Du\otimes Du$. This matrix has eigenvalue $1+|Du|^2$ in the direction of $Du$ and eigenvalue $1$ in the orthogonal directions; if $Du=0$, it is the identity. Thus $J_ mDF=\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}$. Apply Theorem 3.2.2 . $\square$ Theorem 3.2.4 (Coarea formula) . 5830576492D6 Let $V\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$ be open, let $1\leq m<n$, let $f:V\to \mathbb {R}^ m$ be locally Lipschitz, and let $A\subset V$ be Lebesgue measurable. Then the fiber measure on the right is Lebesgue measurable and \[  \int _ A J_ mDf(x)\, d\mathcal{L}^ n(x) =\int _{\mathbb {R}^ m}\mathcal{H}^{n-m}\bigl (A\cap f^{-1}(\{ y\} )\bigr )\, d\mathcal{L}^ m(y).  \] Cited theorem; proof to be added. This is the Euclidean special case of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, equation (2.8), p. 93; Chapter 2, Section 7 develops the smooth case. Compare the rectifiable-set coarea theorem in [ Fed69 ] , Theorem 3.2.22, p. 258. Unlike the area formula, the Jacobian here is $\sqrt{\det (Df(Df)^*)}$.

title: Definition 3.2.1 (Area and coarea Jacobians)
text: Definition 3.2.1 (Area and coarea Jacobians) . ECFDA4F8C960 For a linear map $L:\mathbb {R}^ m\to \mathbb {R}^ n$ with $m\leq n$, define its area Jacobian by \[  J_ mL=\sqrt{\det (L^*L)}.  \] For $L:\mathbb {R}^ n\to \mathbb {R}^ m$ with $m\leq n$, define its coarea Jacobian by \[  J_ mL=\sqrt{\det (LL^*)}.  \] Here $L^*$ is the Euclidean adjoint. Each quantity is zero when $L$ has rank less than $m$. For a locally Lipschitz map, use the appropriate expression with $L=Df(x)$ at points of differentiability, and set it to zero on the exceptional null set. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, equation (3.2), p. 57, and Chapter 3, equation (2.7), p. 93.

title: 4.1 Finite perimeter and reduced boundary
text:
A topological boundary can change drastically when a null set is added. The distributional derivative of the characteristic function provides a boundary notion that depends only on the measurable set. Fleming describes the development of this approach in [ Fle16 ] , Section 3, pp. 3–4. The precise statements below follow [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Section 2, and Chapter 3, Section 4. Definition 4.1.1 (Locally bounded variation) . 4FF0E8DA6480 For $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and an open set $W\subset U$, put \[  |Du|(W)=\sup \left\{ \int _ W u\, \operatorname {div}X\, d\mathcal{L}^ n: X\in C_ c^1(W;\mathbb {R}^ n),\  |X|\leq 1ight\} .  \] We say $u\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ if this quantity is finite for every $W\Subset U$. Equivalently, its distributional derivative $Du$ is a vector-valued Radon measure, characterized by \[  \int _ U u\, \operatorname {div}X\, d\mathcal{L}^ n=-\int _ U X\cdot dDu.  \] The notation $|Du|$ then denotes its total variation measure. We write $u\in BV(U)$ when $u\in L^1(U)$ and $|Du|(U)<\infty $. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Section 2, pp. 52–53. Definition 4.1.2 (Finite perimeter) . 4E14BC795E12 A Lebesgue measurable set $E\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$ has locally finite perimeter in $U$ if $\chi _ E\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Its perimeter in an open set $W\subset U$ is \[  P(E;W)=|D\chi _ E|(W).  \] It has finite perimeter in $U$ if $P(E;U)<\infty $; this does not require $\mathcal{L}^ n(E\cap U)<\infty $. Sets equal almost everywhere have the same distributional derivative and perimeter. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, p. 96. Proposition 4.1.3 (Lower semicontinuity of perimeter) . D59D0CB3A71F Suppose $\chi _{E_ j}	o \chi _ E$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. For every open $W\subset U$, \[  P(E;W)\leq \liminf _{j	o \infty }P(E_ j;W),  \] where the variational definition permits value $+\infty $ even before local finite perimeter is known. Proof For every $X\in C_ c^1(W;\mathbb {R}^ n)$ with $|X|\leq 1$, local $L^1$ convergence and boundedness of $\operatorname {div}X$ give \[  \int _ W\chi _ E\operatorname {div}X\, d\mathcal{L}^ n =\lim _ j\int _ W\chi _{E_ j}\operatorname {div}X\, d\mathcal{L}^ n \leq \liminf _ j P(E_ j;W).  \] Take the supremum over $X$. This is the variational lower semicontinuity used in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Section 2. $\square$ Definition 4.1.4 (Reduced boundary and outward normal) . 55A210572AB4 Let $E$ have locally finite perimeter in $U$. Its reduced boundary $\partial ^*E\cap U$ consists of points $x\in U\cap \operatorname {supp}|D\chi _ E|$ for which \[  v_ E(x)=\lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{D\chi _ E(B_ r(x))}{|D\chi _ E|(B_ r(x))}  \] exists and has length one. We define the outward measure-theoretic unit normal by $
u _ E(x)=-v_ E(x)$. For small $r$ the balls lie in $U$; membership in the support ensures that their denominators are positive. This is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, equations (4.2)–(4.3), pp. 96–97, with the sign reversed to use the outward normal. Theorem 4.1.5 (De Giorgi structure and Gauss–Green) . DA1827FB809A Let $n\geq 2$ and let $E$ have locally finite perimeter in $U\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$. Then $\partial ^*E\cap U$ is countably $(n-1)$-rectifiable and \[  |D\chi _ E|=\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\llcorner (\partial ^*E\cap U), \qquad D\chi _ E=-
u _ E\, \mathcal{H}^{n-1}\llcorner (\partial ^*E\cap U).  \] Consequently, for every $X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb {R}^ n)$, \[  \int _ E\operatorname {div}X\, d\mathcal{L}^ n =\int _{\partial ^*E\cap U}X\cdot 
u _ E\, d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}.  \] Here $X$ is extended by zero outside $U$. The boundary measures in these identities are taken inside $U$. Cited structure theorem; its proof remains to be added. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 4.4, pp. 97–100. The Gauss–Green identity follows immediately from the measure representation and Definition 4.1.1 . The historical account in [ Fle16 ] , Section 3, uses the same outward-normal convention as this entry. Example 4.1.6 (Smooth domains) . 589B34B9A3FE Let $E\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$ be a bounded open set with compact $C^1$ boundary. The classical divergence theorem identifies \[  D\chi _ E=-
u _ E\, \mathcal{H}^{n-1}\llcorner \partial E, \qquad P(E;U)=\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\partial E\cap U).  \] The continuous outward normal has unit length, so the variation of the displayed vector measure is exactly the displayed surface measure. Thus the variational perimeter agrees with the usual boundary area. This also checks the sign in Theorem 4.1.5 .

title: Definition 4.1.1 (Locally bounded variation)
text: Definition 4.1.1 (Locally bounded variation) . 4FF0E8DA6480 For $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and an open set $W\subset U$, put \[  |Du|(W)=\sup \left\{ \int _ W u\, \operatorname {div}X\, d\mathcal{L}^ n: X\in C_ c^1(W;\mathbb {R}^ n),\  |X|\leq 1\right\} .  \] We say $u\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ if this quantity is finite for every $W\Subset U$. Equivalently, its distributional derivative $Du$ is a vector-valued Radon measure, characterized by \[  \int _ U u\, \operatorname {div}X\, d\mathcal{L}^ n=-\int _ U X\cdot dDu.  \] The notation $|Du|$ then denotes its total variation measure. We write $u\in BV(U)$ when $u\in L^1(U)$ and $|Du|(U)<\infty $. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Section 2, pp. 52–53.

title: Definition 4.1.2 (Finite perimeter)
text: Definition 4.1.2 (Finite perimeter) . 4E14BC795E12 A Lebesgue measurable set $E\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$ has locally finite perimeter in $U$ if $\chi _ E\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Its perimeter in an open set $W\subset U$ is \[  P(E;W)=|D\chi _ E|(W).  \] It has finite perimeter in $U$ if $P(E;U)<\infty $; this does not require $\mathcal{L}^ n(E\cap U)<\infty $. Sets equal almost everywhere have the same distributional derivative and perimeter. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, p. 96.

title: Proposition 4.1.3 (Lower semicontinuity of perimeter)
text: Proposition 4.1.3 (Lower semicontinuity of perimeter) . D59D0CB3A71F Suppose $\chi _{E_ j}\to \chi _ E$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. For every open $W\subset U$, \[  P(E;W)\leq \liminf _{j\to \infty }P(E_ j;W),  \] where the variational definition permits value $+\infty $ even before local finite perimeter is known. Proof For every $X\in C_ c^1(W;\mathbb {R}^ n)$ with $|X|\leq 1$, local $L^1$ convergence and boundedness of $\operatorname {div}X$ give \[  \int _ W\chi _ E\operatorname {div}X\, d\mathcal{L}^ n =\lim _ j\int _ W\chi _{E_ j}\operatorname {div}X\, d\mathcal{L}^ n \leq \liminf _ j P(E_ j;W).  \] Take the supremum over $X$. This is the variational lower semicontinuity used in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Section 2. $\square$

title: Definition 4.1.4 (Reduced boundary and outward normal)
text: Definition 4.1.4 (Reduced boundary and outward normal) . 55A210572AB4 Let $E$ have locally finite perimeter in $U$. Its reduced boundary $\partial ^*E\cap U$ consists of points $x\in U\cap \operatorname {supp}|D\chi _ E|$ for which \[  v_ E(x)=\lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{D\chi _ E(B_ r(x))}{|D\chi _ E|(B_ r(x))}  \] exists and has length one. We define the outward measure-theoretic unit normal by $\nu _ E(x)=-v_ E(x)$. For small $r$ the balls lie in $U$; membership in the support ensures that their denominators are positive. This is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, equations (4.2)–(4.3), pp. 96–97, with the sign reversed to use the outward normal.

title: Theorem 4.1.5 (De Giorgi structure and Gauss–Green)
text: Theorem 4.1.5 (De Giorgi structure and Gauss–Green) . DA1827FB809A Let $n\geq 2$ and let $E$ have locally finite perimeter in $U\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$. Then $\partial ^*E\cap U$ is countably $(n-1)$-rectifiable and \[  |D\chi _ E|=\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\llcorner (\partial ^*E\cap U), \qquad D\chi _ E=-\nu _ E\, \mathcal{H}^{n-1}\llcorner (\partial ^*E\cap U).  \] Consequently, for every $X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb {R}^ n)$, \[  \int _ E\operatorname {div}X\, d\mathcal{L}^ n =\int _{\partial ^*E\cap U}X\cdot \nu _ E\, d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}.  \] Here $X$ is extended by zero outside $U$. The boundary measures in these identities are taken inside $U$. Cited structure theorem; its proof remains to be added. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 4.4, pp. 97–100. The Gauss–Green identity follows immediately from the measure representation and Definition 4.1.1 . The historical account in [ Fle16 ] , Section 3, uses the same outward-normal convention as this entry.

title: Example 4.1.6 (Smooth domains)
text: Example 4.1.6 (Smooth domains) . 589B34B9A3FE Let $E\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$ be a bounded open set with compact $C^1$ boundary. The classical divergence theorem identifies \[  D\chi _ E=-\nu _ E\, \mathcal{H}^{n-1}\llcorner \partial E, \qquad P(E;U)=\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\partial E\cap U).  \] The continuous outward normal has unit length, so the variation of the displayed vector measure is exactly the displayed surface measure. Thus the variational perimeter agrees with the usual boundary area. This also checks the sign in Theorem 4.1.5 .

title: 5.1 Currents and compactness
text: Currents retain orientation and multiplicity. Their weak topology is defined by testing against differential forms. We use [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, and compare the overview in [ Fle16 ] , Sections 4–5. Definition 5.1.1 (Current and boundary) . C87631EB7AA5 Let $\mathcal{D}^ m(U)=C_ c^\infty (U;\Lambda ^ m(\mathbb {R}^ n)^*)$ be the space of smooth compactly supported $m$-forms, with its usual test-function topology. An $m$-current is a continuous linear functional $T:\mathcal{D}^ m(U)\to \mathbb {R}$. For $m\geq 1$ its boundary is the $(m-1)$-current \[  \partial T(\eta )=T(d\eta ),\qquad \eta \in \mathcal{D}^{m-1}(U).  \] For $m=0$ set $\partial T=0$. Weak convergence $T_ j\rightharpoonup T$ means $T_ j(\omega )\to T(\omega )$ for every $\omega \in \mathcal{D}^ m(U)$. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Section 2, pp. 159–161. Proposition 5.1.2 (Boundary squared and weak continuity) . 7D8936D48805 Every current satisfies $\partial (\partial T)=0$. Moreover, $T_ j\rightharpoonup T$ implies $\partial T_ j\rightharpoonup \partial T$. Proof For an admissible test form $\eta $, $\partial ^2T(\eta )=T(d^2\eta )=0$. For a test form $\zeta $ of degree $m-1$, its exterior derivative is again smooth and compactly supported, so $\partial T_ j(\zeta )=T_ j(d\zeta )\to T(d\zeta )=\partial T(\zeta )$. The assertions in dimension zero follow from the convention in Definition 5.1.1 . $\square$ Definition 5.1.3 (Mass and the comass convention) . 1EEA7973F645 The comass of an $m$-covector $\alpha $ is \[  \| \alpha \| _* =\sup \{ |\langle \alpha ,v_1\wedge \cdots \wedge v_ m\rangle |: v_1,\ldots ,v_ m\text{ orthonormal}\} .  \] For $m=0$ it is the absolute value. For an open $W\subset U$ define \[  \mathbf{M}_ W(T)=\sup \{ T(\omega ):\omega \in \mathcal{D}^ m(W), \sup _ x\| \omega (x)\| _*\leq 1\} .  \] Write $\mathbf{M}(T)=\mathbf{M}_ U(T)$. Test forms on $W$ are extended by zero to $U$. We use the comass convention of [ Fed69 ] , Section 1.8, pp. 38–40. Simon initially uses the Euclidean norm on covectors in his mass definition, then discusses this distinction in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Remark 2.7, p. 160. Both conventions agree for the rectifiable currents in Definition 5.1.5 ; they need not agree for arbitrary currents. We will not identify their numerical values without this qualification. Proposition 5.1.4 (Lower semicontinuity of mass) . D219E445117D If $T_ j\rightharpoonup T$ in $U$, then for every open $W\subset U$, \[  \mathbf{M}_ W(T)\leq \liminf _ j\mathbf{M}_ W(T_ j).  \] Proof For each test form $\omega $ in the supremum defining $\mathbf{M}_ W(T)$, $T(\omega )=\lim _ jT_ j(\omega )\leq \liminf _ j\mathbf{M}_ W(T_ j)$. Take the supremum over $\omega $. This proof applies even if the limiting lower bound is infinite. Compare [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Section 2. $\square$ Definition 5.1.5 (Integer rectifiable and integral currents) . 4220ABFF9A31 An $m$-current $T$ in $U$ is locally integer rectifiable if \[  T(\omega )=\int _ M\theta (x)\langle \omega (x),\tau (x)\rangle \, d\mathcal{H}^ m(x),  \] where $M\subset U$ is $\mathcal{H}^ m$-measurable and countably $m$-rectifiable, $\theta :M\to \{ 1,2,\ldots \} $ is measurable with $\int _{M\cap K}\theta \, d\mathcal{H}^ m<\infty $ for every compact $K\subset U$, and $\tau (x)$ is a measurable unit simple $m$-vector orienting $T_ xM$ almost everywhere. For $m=0$ this means a locally finite integer combination of point evaluations. It is locally integral if both $T$ and $\partial T$ are locally integer rectifiable. It is integral with finite mass and boundary mass if also $\mathbf{M}(T)+\mathbf{M}(\partial T)<\infty $. For the displayed representation, $\mathbf{M}_ W(T)=\int _{M\cap W}\theta \, d\mathcal{H}^ m$. The mass formula and representation are cited facts; see [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Definition 3.1 and Remark 3.2(3), pp. 172–173. Local finiteness and integrability are taken in the ambient open set, not merely on compact subsets of $M$. Theorem 5.1.6 (Federer–Fleming compactness) . 558B04F2FD71 Let $1\leq m<n$. Suppose that $T_ j$ are integral $m$-currents in $\mathbb {R}^ n$, their supports lie in one compact set $K$, and \[  \sup _ j\bigl (\mathbf{M}(T_ j)+\mathbf{M}(\partial T_ j)\bigr )<\infty .  \] Then a subsequence converges weakly to an integral current $T$ supported in $K$, and \[  \mathbf{M}(T)\leq \liminf _ k\mathbf{M}(T_{j_ k}),\qquad \mathbf{M}(\partial T)\leq \liminf _ k\mathbf{M}(\partial T_{j_ k}).  \] Cited compactness and closure theorem; proof to be added. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Theorem 3.15, p. 175, with its proof in Section 8, and [ Fle16 ] , Sections 4–5, pp. 5–7. The preservation of integer rectifiability is the substantial conclusion. The inequalities then follow from Propositions 5.1.2 and 5.1.4 .

text: Theorem 5.1.6 (Federer–Fleming compactness) . 558B04F2FD71 Let $1\leq m<n$. title: 5.2 Polyhedral and flat chains
text: The flat norm makes boundary continuous while allowing thin fillings to become small. We begin with integer coefficients and polyhedral chains, following [ WhiCho14 ] , Sections 2.1–2.3. General coefficient groups will require separate hypotheses and are not silently included in the statements here. Definition 5.2.1 (Integer polyhedral chains) . 79AE1902199F The group $\mathcal{P}_ m(\mathbb {R}^ n;\mathbb {Z})$ consists of finite integer sums of oriented compact convex $m$-dimensional polyhedra, modulo subdivision and reversal of orientation. After a common subdivision, a chain can be written $P=\sum _ i a_ i[\sigma _ i]$ with pairwise disjoint relative interiors and with repeated pieces combined. Its mass and boundary are \[  \mathbf{M}(P)=\sum _ i|a_ i|\mathcal{H}^ m(\sigma _ i),\qquad \partial P=\sum _ i a_ i\partial [\sigma _ i],  \] where faces carry their induced orientations. For $m=0$ use counting measure and set the boundary to zero. These constructions respect subdivision, and $\partial ^2P=0$. See [ WhiCho14 ] , Definition 2.4 and equation (2.1), pp. 4–5. Definition 5.2.2 (Flat norm and completion) . 394A15B53A4E For $P\in \mathcal{P}_ m(\mathbb {R}^ n;\mathbb {Z})$, define \[  \mathcal{F}(P)=\inf \{ \mathbf{M}(R)+\mathbf{M}(S): R\in \mathcal{P}_ m(\mathbb {R}^ n;\mathbb {Z}), S\in \mathcal{P}_{m+1}(\mathbb {R}^ n;\mathbb {Z}),\  P=R+\partial S\} .  \] When $m=n$, the group of $(n+1)$-chains is zero. This flat norm is symmetric, subadditive, and vanishes only at zero, so $d(P,Q)=\mathcal F(P-Q)$ is a translation-invariant metric; a proof is given in Proposition 5.3.16 . For a compact set $K$, let $\mathcal{P}_ m(K)$ be the chains supported in $K$, with the ambient flat norm. The compactly supported flat chains are the union over compact $K$ of the metric completions of $\mathcal{P}_ m(K)$, using the natural inclusions. This is the convention of [ WhiCho14 ] , equation (2.2) and the discussion on pp. 5–6. The fillings in the displayed infimum are not required to lie in $K$. Proposition 5.2.3 (Boundary is continuous in the flat norm) . FEAB4217D841 For every integer polyhedral chain $P$, \[  \mathcal{F}(P)\leq \mathbf{M}(P),\qquad \mathcal{F}(\partial P)\leq \mathcal{F}(P).  \] The boundary therefore extends continuously to the completions in Definition 5.2.2 . See [ WhiCho14 ] , Section 2.3, pp. 6–8. Proof Take $R=P$ and $S=0$ for the first inequality. If $P=R+\partial S$, then $\partial P=\partial R$. In the definition of $\mathcal{F}(\partial P)$ use residual chain zero and filling $R$. Thus $\mathcal{F}(\partial P)\leq \mathbf{M}(R)\leq \mathbf{M}(R)+\mathbf{M}(S)$. Take the infimum over decompositions of $P$. Applying the same estimate to differences gives the continuous extension on each completion. $\square$ Example 5.2.4 (Thin boundaries and loss of mass) . 2113703E7856 In $\mathbb {R}^2$ let $Q_\varepsilon $ be the oriented rectangle $[0,1]\times [0,\varepsilon ]$, with $\varepsilon >0$. Then \[  \mathcal{F}(\partial Q_\varepsilon )\leq \mathbf{M}(Q_\varepsilon )=\varepsilon , \qquad \mathbf{M}(\partial Q_\varepsilon )=2+2\varepsilon .  \] Thus $\partial Q_\varepsilon $ converges to zero in the flat norm as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, although its mass tends to $2$. The first estimate uses $Q_\varepsilon $ as a filling and the second sums its four edge lengths. This is the example in [ WhiCho14 ] , Example 2.7, p. 6. Flat convergence does not imply convergence of mass.

title: 6.1 Varifolds and first variation
text: A varifold records location and an unoriented tangent plane. This formulation places smooth and nonsmooth surfaces in a common space of Radon measures. We use [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 8, Sections 1–3. Definition 6.1.1 (Varifold and weight) . 4CCDC6F2267C Let $1\leq m<n$. The Grassmannian $G(n,m)$ is the space of unoriented $m$-dimensional linear subspaces of $\mathbb {R}^ n$, with the topology induced by the orthogonal projection matrices. An $m$-varifold in $U$ is a nonnegative Radon measure on $G_ m(U)=U\times G(n,m)$. Its weight is the Radon measure on $U$ defined by \[  \| V\| (A)=V(A\times G(n,m))\qquad (A\subset U\text{ Borel}).  \] Varifold convergence means weak convergence of these measures against $C_ c(G_ m(U))$. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 8, Section 1, pp. 235–236. Definition 6.1.2 (Rectifiable and integral varifolds) . 46E46AD2EF79 Let $M\subset U$ be $\mathcal{H}^ m$-measurable and countably $m$-rectifiable, with locally finite $\mathcal{H}^ m$ measure in $U$. Let $\theta :M\to (0,\infty )$ be measurable and satisfy $\int _{M\cap K}\theta \, d\mathcal{H}^ m<\infty $ for every compact $K\subset U$. The associated rectifiable varifold $V(M,\theta )$ is determined by \[  \int \varphi (x,S)\, dV(M,\theta )(x,S) =\int _ M\varphi (x,T_ xM)\theta (x)\, d\mathcal{H}^ m(x).  \] It is integral if $\theta $ is integer-valued almost everywhere. Its weight is $\theta \mathcal{H}^ m\llcorner M$. The tangent planes exist almost everywhere by Theorem 3.1.4 ; changing the integrand on the exceptional null set has no effect. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 4, Section 1, and Chapter 8, p. 236. Definition 6.1.3 (First variation, stationarity, and mean curvature) . CBCB798B764C For an $m$-varifold $V$ and $X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb {R}^ n)$, define \[  \delta V(X)=\int _{G_ m(U)}\operatorname {div}_ S X(x)\, dV(x,S),\qquad \operatorname {div}_ S X=\sum _{i=1}^ m\langle D_{e_ i}X,e_ i\rangle ,  \] where $(e_ i)$ is any orthonormal basis of $S$. The trace is independent of that basis. We call $V$ stationary in $U$ if $\delta V(X)=0$ for every such $X$. It has locally bounded first variation if for each $W\Subset U$ there is $C_ W<\infty $ such that $|\delta V(X)|\leq C_ W\sup |X|$ whenever $X$ is supported in $W$. In the case when the first variation is represented entirely by a vector field $H\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\| V\| ;\mathbb {R}^ n)$, \[  \delta V(X)=-\int _ U H\cdot X\, d\| V\| ,  \] we call $H$ the generalized mean curvature. Locally bounded first variation alone may also have a singular boundary term; the last identity assumes that term is absent. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 8, equations (2.3)–(2.10), pp. 239–240. Proposition 6.1.4 (An affine plane is stationary) . B47686B92774 Let $P\subset \mathbb {R}^ n$ be an affine $m$-plane and let $\theta >0$ be constant. Then $V(P,\theta )$ is stationary in $\mathbb {R}^ n$. Proof Identify $P$ isometrically with $\mathbb {R}^ m$. The restriction of a compactly supported vector field has compact support on $P$, and its tangential divergence is the Euclidean divergence of its tangential component. The integral of each coordinate derivative is zero by the fundamental theorem of calculus and Fubini's theorem. Hence $\delta V(X)=\theta \int _ P\operatorname {div}_ P X\, d\mathcal{H}^ m=0$. $\square$ Theorem 6.1.5 (Stationary monotonicity) . A08B64B5DD43 Let $V$ be a stationary $m$-varifold in $U$, let $a\in U$, and suppose $\overline{B_ R(a)}\subset U$. Then \[  r\longmapsto \frac{\| V\| (B_ r(a))}{\omega _ mr^ m} \quad \text{is nondecreasing for }0<r<R.  \] Consequently $\Theta ^ m(\| V\| ,a)$ exists and is finite and nonnegative. No rectifiability hypothesis is needed for this conclusion, and the density may be zero. Cited monotonicity theorem; proof to be added. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 8, Section 3, equations (3.5)–(3.6), p. 241, with $\Lambda =0$. Finiteness of the limiting density follows by bounding all sufficiently small ratios by the ratio at any fixed radius less than $R$ and using local finiteness of $\| V\| $.

title: 7.1 Minimal hypersurfaces and stability
text:
In the variational chapters we write $M^{n+1}$ for the ambient manifold and $\Sigma ^ n$ for a hypersurface. Thus $n$ is the hypersurface dimension. A surface has $n=2$. These conventions replace the Euclidean dimension letters used in the foundational chapters. The smooth theory connects the first variation of varifolds with elliptic equations and Morse index. Sources for this section are Marques' lectures, recorded by Montezuma, [ MM ] , Sections 2 and 6, and Chodosh [ ChMin ] , Sections 7 and 23. Definition 7.1.1 (Mean curvature and minimality) . 28E53582FC82 For a smooth immersed hypersurface $\Sigma \subset M$, let \[  B(X,Y)=(
abla ^ M_ XY)^\perp ,\qquad \vec H=\operatorname {tr}_{T\Sigma }B.  \] We call $\Sigma $ minimal when $\vec H=0$. If a global unit normal $
u $ exists, $\Sigma $ is two-sided. Our scalar convention is $H=\operatorname {div}_{\Sigma }
u $, so that $\vec H=-H
u $. With the outward normal, a Euclidean sphere of radius $R$ has $H=n/R$. Here $H$ is the sum of principal curvatures; in the Willmore energy we explicitly use their average. See [ MM ] , Section 2, and [ ChMin ] , Section 7. Proposition 7.1.2 (First variation of a closed hypersurface) . 571E6CF1470F Let $\Sigma $ be smooth, compact, and without boundary. If $F_ t$ is a smooth variation with velocity $X$, then \[  \left. rac{d}{dt}ight|_{0}\operatorname {Area}(F_ t(\Sigma )) =\int _\Sigma \operatorname {div}_\Sigma X\, dA =-\int _\Sigma \langle \vec H,Xangle \, dA.  \] For $X=f
u $ this equals $\int _\Sigma Hf\, dA$. This is the smooth counterpart of the varifold first variation. Compare [ MM ] , Theorems 2.3 and 2.6. Proof In local coordinates, differentiating the induced metric gives $\dot g_{ij}=\langle 
abla _ iX,e_ jangle +\langle e_ i,
abla _ jXangle $. The identity $ rac{d}{dt}\sqrt{\det g}= rac12\operatorname {tr}(g^{-1}\dot g)\sqrt{\det g}$ therefore gives $\dot{dA}=\operatorname {div}_\Sigma X\, dA$. Decompose $X=X^ T+X^\perp $. Differentiating $\langle X^\perp ,e_ iangle =0$ along an orthonormal tangent frame yields $\operatorname {div}_\Sigma X=\operatorname {div}_\Sigma X^ T-\langle \vec H,Xangle $. The tangential divergence integrates to zero because $\Sigma $ has no boundary. Finally substitute $\vec H=-H
u $. $\square$ Theorem 7.1.3 (Second variation in the two-sided case) . 30FBA471ADE5 Let $\Sigma ^ n\subset (M^{n+1},g)$ be a smooth, closed, two-sided minimal hypersurface. For a smooth normal variation with initial velocity $f
u $, the second derivative of area is \[  Q(f,f)=\int _\Sigma  igl (|
abla _\Sigma f|^2-(|B|^2+\operatorname {Ric}_ M(
u ,
u ))f^2 igr )\, dA.  \] With $\Delta _\Sigma =\operatorname {div}_\Sigma 
abla _\Sigma $, define $J=\Delta _\Sigma +|B|^2+\operatorname {Ric}_ M(

At a minimal initial hypersurface, the terms from differentiating $f_ t$ and $dA_ t$ vanish because $H_0=0$. Thus $A''(0)=\int _\Sigma f\dot H$. The Riemannian calculation in Proposition 11.3.4 , which does not use the second variation, gives $\dot H=-\Delta _\Sigma f-(|B|^2+\operatorname {Ric}(

u ))f$. Integration by parts on the closed hypersurface proves the formula. A tangential initial velocity contributes the tangential derivative of $H_0=0$, so only the normal speed enters. The same proof works for variations compactly supported away from a boundary. $\square$ Definition 7.1.4 (Stability and Morse index) . 6E18930B316D For the hypersurface in Theorem 7.1.3 , stability means $Q(f,f)\geq 0$ for every smooth $f$. The Morse index is the largest dimension of a linear subspace on which $Q$ is negative definite. A Jacobi field is a normal field in the kernel of the Jacobi operator. For a one-sided hypersurface, use sections of its normal line bundle, equivalently the appropriate equivariant functions on the two-sided cover. title: 7.2 Minimal graphs and elliptic regularity
text: The graph equation is a first bridge from geometric variation to nonlinear elliptic PDE. Simon's supplied Lectures on PDE , last updated March 5, 2015, develops the analytic background and treats the minimal surface and mean curvature equations in Chapter 19 [ SimonPDE ] . Proposition 7.2.1 (The minimal graph equation) . 118E021473BF Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be open and $u\in C^2(U)$. The graph of $u$ is stationary for compactly supported vertical variations if and only if \[  \operatorname {div}\left(\frac{Du}{\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}}\right)=0.  \] Equivalently, $\bigl (\delta _{ij}-u_ i u_ j/(1+|Du|^2)\bigr )u_{ij}=0$, where repeated indices are summed. Compare [ SimonPDE ] , Chapter 19, and [ ChMin ] , Section 18. Proof For a relatively compact domain containing the support of a test function $\phi $, the graph area is $\int \sqrt{1+|Du|^2}$ by the area formula. Its derivative at $u+t\phi $ is $\int Du\cdot D\phi /\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}$. Integration by parts gives the stated equation. Expanding the divergence gives the nondivergence expression. Since $u$ is $C^2$, the weak and pointwise expressions agree. $\square$ Remark 7.2.2 (Regularity techniques and their hypotheses) . 5BFC45FF0297 The analytic and geometric regularity inputs are developed separately below. Definitions 7.2.3 and 7.5.2 specify weak equations; Proposition 7.2.4 identifies the gradient bound that gives uniform ellipticity. Theorems 7.5.6 and 7.5.8 provide distinct estimates for measurable and Hölder coefficients. The graph comparison and calibration results then give geometric consequences. For nonsmooth varifolds, Theorem 6.3.6 constructs blow-ups, Theorem 6.4.3 states the density and mean-curvature hypotheses for Allard regularity, and Theorem 7.6.6 gives a low-dimensional stable curvature estimate. Their sources are [ SimonPDE ] , [ ChMin ] , and [ Minter ] . These results do not assert unrestricted regularity for stationary varifolds; cylindrical-cone and general sheeting theories still require their own development. Definition 7.2.3 (Weak minimal graphs) . 2BE9138D926B A function $u\in W^{1,\infty }_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ open, is a weak solution of the scalar minimal surface equation if \[  \int _ U F(Du)\cdot D\phi =0\quad (\phi \in C_ c^\infty (U)), \qquad F(p)=\frac p{\sqrt{1+|p|^2}}.  \] The integrand is locally integrable, so the equation is defined without second derivatives. Here the graph has codimension one. See [ Minter ] , Section 3.1, p. 48. Proposition 7.2.4 (Ellipticity and the gradient bound) . 29B464EBCF55 For $F$ in Definition 7.2.3 , write $W(p)=\sqrt{1+|p|^2}$. Then \[  A_{ij}(p)=\partial _{p_ j}F_ i(p)=\frac{\delta _{ij}}{W(p)}-\frac{p_ i p_ j}{W(p)^3}.  \] Its eigenvalues are $W^{-1}$ on $p^\perp $ and $W^{-3}$ in the direction of $p$; at $p=0$ they are all one. Consequently, when $|p|\leq L$, \[  (1+L^2)^{-3/2}|\xi |^2\leq A(p)\xi \cdot \xi \leq |\xi |^2.  \] The nondivergence coefficient matrix $a(p)=W(p)A(p)$ has eigenvalues $1$ and $(1+|p|^2)^{-1}$. These ellipticity constants deteriorate as the gradient grows. Compare [ ChMin ] , Exercise 18.1. Proof Differentiate $p_ i(1+|p|^2)^{-1/2}$. Decompose $\xi $ into its components parallel and perpendicular to $p$. The displayed eigenvalues and bounds follow directly. $\square$ Proposition 7.2.5 (Linearization and differences of graph solutions) . 65270DE0F6E0 For a smooth $u$, the linearization of $u\mapsto \operatorname {div}F(Du)$ in direction $v$ is $\operatorname {div}(A(Du)Dv)$. If $u_1,u_2$ are smooth minimal graph solutions, their difference $w=u_2-u_1$ satisfies \[  \operatorname {div}(\overline A Dw)=0,\qquad \overline A(x)=\int _0^1 A\bigl ((1-t)Du_1(x)+tDu_2(x)\bigr )\, dt.  \] If both gradients have norm at most $L$, then $\overline A$ has the bounds in Proposition 7.2.4 . In particular each derivative $D_ k u$ of a smooth solution satisfies $\operatorname {div}(A(Du)D(D_ k u))=0$. Proof Differentiate $F(Du+tDv)$ under the divergence. For two solutions, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $F(Du_2)-F(Du_1)=\overline A Dw$; take its divergence. The segment between the two gradients stays in the ball of radius $L$, so averaging preserves the ellipticity bounds. Differentiating the equation in $x_ k$ gives the last claim. This is the divergence-form counterpart of the linearization in [ ChMin ] , Proposition 19.3. $\square$ Theorem 7.2.6 (Smoothness of Lipschitz weak minimal graphs) . 86FA24C083FB Every locally Lipschitz weak solution of the scalar minimal surface equation on an open $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ has a smooth representative in $U$. No smallness of its Lipschitz constant is required locally. This scalar result does not extend as stated to arbitrary higher-codimension minimal graph systems. The proof uses difference quotients, uniform ellipticity on compact subsets, De Giorgi–Nash–Moser regularity for derivatives, and Schauder bootstrapping. Sources: [ Minter ] , Section 3.1, and the discussion following Theorem 2.5; [ SimonPDE ] , Chapters 18–19. The weak-solution regularity proof remains external. Proposition 7.2.7 (Bootstrapping a classical minimal graph) . 9843EEC0DB02 A $C^2$ solution of the minimal surface equation on $U$ belongs to $C^\infty (U)$. Proof On nested relatively compact balls the gradient is bounded, and the coefficients $a^{ij}(Du)$ are $C^1$, hence Hölder continuous for every exponent below one. Apply Theorem 7.5.8 to $a^{ij}(Du)D_{ij}u=0$ to obtain $u\in C^{2,\alpha }_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Differentiation gives \[  a^{ij}(Du)D_{ij}(D_ k u)+ \bigl (\partial _{p_\ell }a^{ij}(Du)D_{ij}u\bigr )D_\ell (D_ k u)=0.  \] The lower-order coefficients are $C^{0,\alpha }$. Interior Schauder regularity gives one further derivative, with the differentiated equation justified by difference quotients if needed. Repeating on smaller balls proves the claim. This is the bootstrap in [ ChMin ] , Lemma 19.1, pp. 51–52. $\square$ Proposition 7.2.8 (Strong comparison for minimal graphs) . EA3CB199A4FD Let $U$ be connected, and let $u_1,u_2\in C^2(U)$ solve the minimal surface equation. If $u_1\leq u_2$ in $U$ and equality holds at one interior point, then $u_1=u_2$ throughout $U$. Proof The solutions are smooth by Proposition 7.2.7 . Their nonnegative difference solves the locally uniformly elliptic equation in Proposition 7.2.5 . On a sufficiently small ball about a zero, Harnack gives $\sup w\leq C\inf w=0$. Thus the zero set is open; it is also closed by continuity. Connectedness completes the proof. Compare [ ChMin ] , Proposition 19.3. $\square$ Corollary 7.2.9 (Boundary comparison and uniqueness) . AF64217A81F7 Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be a bounded connected domain. Suppose $u_1,u_2\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\overline U)$ are minimal graph solutions and $u_1\leq u_2$ on $\partial U$. Then $u_1\leq u_2$ in $U$. In particular a classical solution with prescribed continuous boundary values is unique, when it exists. Proof If $t=\max _{\overline U}(u_1-u_2)>0$, the maximum is attained in $U$. The functions $u_1$ and $u_2+t$ are ordered solutions with interior contact, so Proposition 7.2.8 makes them equal throughout $U$. Continuity at the boundary contradicts the boundary inequality. This is the sliding argument of [ ChMin ] , Corollary 19.4. $\square$ Corollary 7.2.10 (Interior tangency principle) . DBF134AFFBB2 Let two smooth embedded minimal hypersurfaces in a smooth Riemannian manifold touch at an interior point. If one lies locally on one side of the other, then their supports agree in a neighborhood of that point. Proof Use a common tangent plane and a coordinate chart to write both hypersurfaces as graphs. Their difference is nonnegative and solves the linear uniformly elliptic equation obtained by integrating the linearization of the local mean-curvature operator between the graphs. The coefficients are smooth and bounded on a smaller chart. The interior Harnack principle for this equation, including its bounded lower-order coefficients, forces the difference to vanish. See [ ChMin ] , Section 19, and [ SimonPDE ] , Chapter 18, Theorem 1. The hypothesis is interior one-sided contact; transverse crossings do not satisfy it. $\square$ Definition 7.2.11 (Calibrations) . 5CC331303E30 On an oriented Riemannian manifold, a calibration of degree $n$ is a smooth closed $n$-form $\omega $ with comass at most one at every point. An oriented immersed $n$-submanifold $\Sigma $ is calibrated when $\omega |_{T\Sigma }=dA_\Sigma $. The comass is the supremum of the absolute value on unit simple $n$-vectors, as in Definition 5.1.3 . See [ ChMin ] , Section 16. Proposition 7.2.12 (A calibration proves area minimization) . 27EE3D841187 Let $\Sigma $ and $S$ be compact oriented smooth $n$-submanifolds with the same oriented boundary in an open set $U$, and suppose $S-\Sigma =\partial R$ for a compactly supported $(n+1)$-current $R$ in $U$. If a calibration $\omega $ on $U$ calibrates $\Sigma $, then $\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )\leq \operatorname {Area}(S)$. Proof Stokes' theorem and $d\omega =0$ give $\int _ S\omega -\int _\Sigma \omega =R(d\omega )=0$. A cutoff identically one near the compact supports justifies evaluating a possibly noncompactly supported form. The calibration identity gives $\int _\Sigma \omega =\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )$, while the comass bound gives $\int _ S\omega \leq \operatorname {Area}(S)$. Compare [ ChMin ] , Theorem 16.2. $\square$ Proposition 7.2.13 (Minimal graphs are calibrated in their cylinder) . 74F9A2FF880C If $u\in C^2(U)$ solves the minimal surface equation, define on $U\times \mathbb R$ \[  N(x,z)=\frac{(-Du(x),1)}{\sqrt{1+|Du(x)|^2}},\qquad \omega =\iota _ N(dx_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dx_ n\wedge dz).  \] Orient the graph so that $\omega $ restricts to its positive area form. Then $\omega $ calibrates it. Consequently compact portions of the graph minimize area against oriented competitors homologous to them by compactly supported currents inside $U\times \mathbb R$. Proof The normal field has length one, so the comass of $\omega $ is one. Also $d\omega =(\operatorname {div}N)\, dx_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dz=0$ by the graph equation and independence from $z$. On the graph, $N$ is its unit normal, giving the calibration identity. Apply Proposition 7.2.12 . This is [ ChMin ] , Example 16.3 and Theorem 18.1. The cylinder restriction is part of the conclusion. $\square$ Example 7.2.14 (A graph with unbounded slope at its domain boundary) . 62DB8C81E589 On $(-\pi /2,\pi /2)^2$, the function $u(x,y)=\log (\cos y)-\log (\cos x)$ is a minimal graph. Indeed $u_ x=\tan x$, $u_ y=-\tan y$, $u_{xx}=\sec ^2x$, $u_{yy}=-\sec ^2y$, and $u_{xy}=0$, so \[  (1+u_ y^2)u_{xx}-2u_ xu_ yu_{xy}+(1+u_ x^2)u_{yy}=0.  \] Its slope is bounded on compact subsets but diverges near the square's boundary. Thus local ellipticity does not give a single uniform ellipticity constant on the entire domain. Compare [ ChMin ] , Exercise 18.2.

title: Proposition 7.2.1 (The minimal graph equation)
text: Proposition 7.2.1 (The minimal graph equation) . 118E021473BF Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be open and $u\in C^2(U)$. The graph of $u$ is stationary for compactly supported vertical variations if and only if \[  \operatorname {div}\left(\frac{Du}{\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}}\right)=0.  \] Equivalently, $\bigl (\delta _{ij}-u_ i u_ j/(1+|Du|^2)\bigr )u_{ij}=0$, where repeated indices are summed. Compare [ SimonPDE ] , Chapter 19, and [ ChMin ] , Section 18. Proof For a relatively compact domain containing the support of a test function $\phi $, the graph area is $\int \sqrt{1+|Du|^2}$ by the area formula. Its derivative at $u+t\phi $ is $\int Du\cdot D\phi /\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}$. Integration by parts gives the stated equation. Expanding the divergence gives the nondivergence expression. Since $u$ is $C^2$, the weak and pointwise expressions agree. $\square$

title: Remark 7.2.2 (Regularity techniques and their hypotheses)
text: Remark 7.2.2 (Regularity techniques and their hypotheses) . 5BFC45FF0297 The analytic and geometric regularity inputs are developed separately below. Definitions 7.2.3 and 7.5.2 specify weak equations; Proposition 7.2.4 identifies the gradient bound that gives uniform ellipticity. Theorems 7.5.6 and 7.5.8 provide distinct estimates for measurable and Hölder coefficients. The graph comparison and calibration results then give geometric consequences. For nonsmooth varifolds, Theorem 6.3.6 constructs blow-ups, Theorem 6.4.3 states the density and mean-curvature hypotheses for Allard regularity, and Theorem 7.6.6 gives a low-dimensional stable curvature estimate. Their sources are [ SimonPDE ] , [ ChMin ] , and [ Minter ] . These results do not assert unrestricted regularity for stationary varifolds; cylindrical-cone and general sheeting theories still require their own development.

title: 8.1 Cycles and min-max families
text: Pitts' monograph [ Pitts81 ] is the foundational source for discrete homotopies, almost minimizing varifolds, and regularity. We introduce the continuous notation used by Marques–Neves [ MNIndex ] , Sections 1–2, and use Li's July 7, 2019 preliminary notes [ LiAP ] as a guide to the discrete construction. A homotopy-class width and a volume-spectrum width are different definitions. Definition 8.1.1 (Mod-two boundary cycles and topologies) . AEAF42CA9912 Let $(M^{n+1},g)$ be smooth, closed, and connected, with $n\geq 1$. Write $\mathcal Z_ n^0(M;\mathbb Z_2)$ for the flat component of zero in the space of integral mod-two $n$-cycles: these are boundaries $T=\partial U$ of mod-two $(n+1)$-chains. We use $\mathcal F$ for the flat metric, $\mathbf M$ for mass, and $\mathbf F_ V$ for a metric inducing weak varifold convergence on bounded-mass sets. Set \[  \mathbf F(T,S)=\mathcal F(T-S)+\mathbf F_ V(|T|,|S|).  \] Here $|T|$ is the associated unoriented varifold. The flat topology can lose area by cancellation, while the varifold term records area and tangent planes. Source: [ MNIndex ] , Section 2. The integer currents of the foundational chapter and these mod-two boundary cycles have different coefficient conventions. Definition 8.1.2 (A fixed homotopy-class width) . 073350371C3C Let $X$ be a finite simplicial complex and $\Phi :X\to \mathcal Z_ n^0(M;\mathbb Z_2)$ be $\mathbf F$-continuous. Let $\Pi $ contain all $\mathbf F$-continuous maps from $X$ that are homotopic to $\Phi $ in the flat topology. Its width is \[  \mathbf L(\Pi )=\inf _{\Psi \in \Pi }\sup _{x\in X}\mathbf M(\Psi (x)).  \] A minimizing sequence $\Phi _ i\in \Pi $ has maximal masses converging to $\mathbf L(\Pi )$. Its critical set consists of varifold limits of slices $|\Phi _{i_ j}(x_ j)|$ whose masses converge to $\mathbf L(\Pi )$. This is the convention of [ MNIndex ] , Section 1. The discrete homotopy formulation in [ Pitts81 ] , Section 4.1, requires a separate interpolation argument to compare the constructions. Definition 8.1.3 (Mass fineness of a discrete family) . 92950BF01F3D On the vertices of a finite cubical subdivision, a map $\phi $ to cycles has mass fineness \[  \mathbf f(\phi )=\max \{ \mathbf M(\phi (x)-\phi (y)):x,y\text{ are adjacent vertices}\} .  \] Almgren–Pitts sequences use successively finer subdivisions, uniformly bounded masses, and fineness tending to zero; their homotopies must satisfy corresponding fineness conditions. Small flat distances alone do not supply these conditions. Sources: [ Pitts81 ] , Section 4.1; [ LiAP ] , Section 4.1; [ LMN ] , Section 2.9. Remark 8.1.4 (Smooth sweepouts in dimension three) . E05332744D17 Colding–De Lellis [ CDL ] , Section 1.1, formulate one-parameter families of surfaces on a closed three-manifold and allow specified degenerations at finitely many points. Their saturated classes are closed under parameter-dependent ambient isotopies. This provides a geometric route to the pull-tight and replacement arguments, alongside Pitts' cycle-space formulation. The parameter space, allowed degenerations, and saturation condition are part of that construction; they must be checked before transferring a width or a genus conclusion to another setting. The author's publication page also lists an erratum, which should be consulted when importing detailed proofs from this survey.

title: 8.2 Almost minimizing varifolds and existence
text: A critical limit needs more than stationarity. Pitts arranges that it resists small local mass-decreasing deformations in annuli; replacement arguments then connect this variational condition to regularity. Definition 8.2.1 (Almost minimizing in an open set) . 5A3BD49B3997 Fix an open $U\subset M$ and $\varepsilon ,\delta >0$. A mod-two cycle $T$ is $(\varepsilon ,\delta )$-almost minimizing in $U$ in the mass formulation if every finite sequence $T=T_0,\ldots ,T_ q$ of cycles with \[  \operatorname {spt}(T_ i-T)\subset U,\quad \mathbf M(T_ i-T_{i-1})\leq \delta ,\quad \mathbf M(T_ i)\leq \mathbf M(T)+\delta  \] satisfies $\mathbf M(T_ q)\geq \mathbf M(T)-\varepsilon $. A varifold $V$ is almost minimizing in $U$ in this formulation if for every $\varepsilon >0$ some $\delta >0$ and such a $T$ satisfy $\mathbf F_ V(V,|T|)<\varepsilon $. The annular condition requires, for every $p\in M$, a radius $r_ p>0$ such that this property holds in each $B_ t(p)\setminus \overline B_ s(p)$ with $0<s<t<r_ p$. Compare [ LiAP ] , Definition 2.1 and Theorem 2.2, and [ Pitts81 ] , Sections 3.1–3.9. The cited sources compare flat and mass formulations after restricting to smaller open sets; those equivalence proofs are not included here. Theorem 8.2.2 (Pitts' original smooth existence range) . 0B2FDF2F71CE Every smooth closed Riemannian manifold $M^{n+1}$ with $2\leq n\leq 5$ contains a nonempty smooth closed embedded minimal hypersurface. This is the smooth-metric specialization of [ Pitts81 ] , Introduction, Theorem A, and Theorem 7.13. Pitts' proof is an external dependency. This statement records the dimension range in the supplied book; later regularity extensions are not being attributed to that original statement. Theorem 8.2.3 (Realization of a positive homotopy width) . 05D114DEC261 Let $M^{n+1}$ be smooth, closed, and connected, with $2\leq n\leq 6$. Let $\Pi $ and a minimizing sequence be as in Definition 8.1.2 , and suppose $\mathbf L(\Pi )>0$. The critical set contains an integral varifold \[  V=\sum _{j=1}^ N m_ j|\Sigma _ j|,\qquad \| V\| (M)=\mathbf L(\Pi ),  \] where the $m_ j$ are positive integers and the $\Sigma _ j$ are pairwise disjoint smooth closed embedded minimal hypersurfaces. This modern formulation, including the Schoen–Simon regularity input, is stated in [ MNIndex ] , Section 1, p. 4; see also [ LiAP ] , Section 5. Its proof remains external. Neither connectedness nor multiplicity one is part of this conclusion. Remark 8.2.4 (The proof dependencies in Pitts' construction) . F06EA6D2D607 The source route is: discrete homotopies and a nontrivial class ( [ Pitts81 ] , Sections 4.1–4.7), pull-tight to obtain stationarity (Section 4.3), the combinatorial argument producing almost minimizing critical limits (Sections 4.8–4.13), and replacement and regularity arguments (Chapters 5–7). Li [ LiAP ] , Sections 3–5, separates the same topological, variational, and analytic steps. Colding–De Lellis [ CDL ] supplies the three-dimensional smooth-family perspective. A deformation that establishes stationarity alone does not complete the regularity step. The detailed proofs of these bridges remain to be written in this reference.

title: 9.1 The volume spectrum and Weyl law
search_title: The volume spectrum and Weyl law
section: 9.1 The volume spectrum and Weyl law
text: In this section $M^{n+1}$ is smooth, closed, and connected, and $n\geq 1$. We use mod-two boundary cycles with the flat topology. The topology of this component provides a distinguished class $\bar\lambda \in H^1(\mathcal Z_ n^0(M;\mathbb Z_2);\mathbb Z_2)$: the nonzero generator whose cup powers detect families. Its identification via Almgren's cycle-space theory is an external topological input; see [ MNIndex ] , Section 5. The supplied published Weyl-law paper [ LMN ] uses flat-continuous families with no concentration of mass. Definition 9.1.1 (No concentration of mass) . F9E567A4EE61 A family $\Phi :X\to \mathcal Z_ n^0(M;\mathbb Z_2)$ has no concentration of mass if \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\sup _{x\in X,\, p\in M} \| \Phi (x)\| (B_ r(p))=0.  \] The supremum over all parameters is essential: the absence of atoms in each individual slice does not give this uniform condition. See [ LMN ] , Section 2.6. Definition 9.1.2 (Sweepouts and the volume spectrum) . 0363383FFC95 For a positive integer $p$, a $p$-sweepout is a flat-continuous map $\Phi :X\to \mathcal Z_ n^0(M;\mathbb Z_2)$ from a finite cubical complex such that $\Phi ^*(\bar\lambda ^ p)\neq 0$ in $H^ p(X;\mathbb Z_2)$. In the present convention admissible sweepouts also have no concentration of mass and bounded maximal mass. Define \[  \omega _ p(M,g)=\inf _\Phi \sup _{x\in X}\mathbf M_ g(\Phi (x)).  \] The infimum permits different parameter complexes and different homotopy classes. Thus $\omega _ p$ is not the width of an arbitrary fixed class $\Pi $. We use the boundary component explicitly, as in [ MNIndex ] , Sections 1 and 5, with the admissibility condition of [ LMN ] , Section 2.6. Comparison with the $\mathbf F$-continuous convention uses interpolation, an external dependency. Lemma 9.1.3 (Monotonicity in the sweepout index) . A3635FA3B0D1 For every $p\geq 1$, $\omega _ p(M,g)\leq \omega _{p+1}(M,g)$. Proof If $\Phi ^*(\bar\lambda ^{p+1})\neq 0$, then $\Phi ^*(\bar\lambda ^ p)$ cannot vanish: multiplying a zero class by $\Phi ^*(\bar\lambda )$ would give zero. Hence every admissible $(p+1)$-sweepout is an admissible $p$-sweepout. Taking the infima in Definition 9.1.2 gives the inequality. This argument gives no strict inequality. $\square$ Lemma 9.1.4 (Scaling of widths) . 0B5B92D679F2 For $r>0$ and $g_ r=r^2g$, \[  \omega _ p(M,g_ r)=r^ n\omega _ p(M,g),\qquad \operatorname {Vol}(M,g_ r)=r^{n+1}\operatorname {Vol}(M,g).  \] Proof The identity on $M$ preserves the flat topology, the component of boundary cycles, and the detecting class. An $n$-dimensional mass is multiplied by $r^ n$; balls of radius $s$ for $g_ r$ are balls of radius $s/r$ for $g$. Thus the no-concentration condition is preserved, and the admissible families are the same. Take their maximal masses and then their infimum. The volume identity follows by scaling the $(n+1)$-dimensional volume element. $\square$ Theorem 9.1.5 (Weyl law for the volume spectrum) . 272A35DD519B For each $n\geq 1$ there is a constant $a(n)>0$, depending only on $n$, such that every smooth closed connected $(M^{n+1},g)$ satisfies \[  \lim _{p\to \infty }p^{-1/(n+1)}\omega _ p(M,g) =a(n)\operatorname {Vol}(M,g)^{n/(n+1)}.  \] This is the closed-manifold case of [ LMN ] , Theorem 1.1, p. 934. The source also treats compact manifolds with boundary using relative cycles. The proof, based on localization and comparison with Euclidean domains, is not yet included. The exponent agrees with Lemma 9.1.4 ; the theorem does not assert an exact formula for any fixed finite $p$.

title: 9.2 Multiplicity and the Morse index
text: The coefficients of a sweepout do not determine the multiplicities of its varifold limit. Index estimates require their own hypotheses in addition to the existence and regularity theory. Definition 9.2.1 (Bumpy metrics and the index of a minimal cycle) . BE8BE104CF66 A smooth metric is bumpy if no smooth closed immersed minimal hypersurface admits a nonzero normal Jacobi field. For an embedded minimal cycle $V=\sum _ j m_ j|\Sigma _ j|$ with distinct disjoint components, define $\operatorname {index}(V)=\sum _ j\operatorname {index}(\Sigma _ j)$; the integers $m_ j$ do not multiply the index. Multiplicity one means that every $m_ j$ is one. This convention is used in [ MNIndex ] , Section 1. A disconnected hypersurface is allowed. Theorem 9.2.2 (Index equality under a critical-set multiplicity hypothesis) . 5CC6B5664356 Let $g$ be a smooth bumpy metric on a closed connected $M^{n+1}$ with $2\leq n\leq 6$. Use the $\mathbf F$-continuous sweepout convention of [ MNIndex ] . Let $\Pi $ be a homotopy class of $p$-sweepouts on a fixed finite $p$-dimensional simplicial complex, with $\mathbf L(\Pi )=\omega _ p(M,g)$, and let $\Phi _ i$ be a minimizing sequence in $\Pi $. Suppose that every embedded minimal cycle in its critical set has multiplicity one. Then that critical set contains an embedded minimal cycle $\Sigma $ satisfying \[  \operatorname {Area}_ g(\Sigma )=\omega _ p(M,g),\qquad \operatorname {index}(\Sigma )=p.  \] Source: [ MNIndex ] , Main Theorem 1.3, p. 5. The proof remains external. The multiplicity assumption concerns the whole indicated critical set, not merely one selected element; this theorem does not by itself prove multiplicity one.

title: 10.1 The Willmore energy and the catenoid estimate
search_title: The Willmore energy and the catenoid estimate
section: 10.1 The Willmore energy and the catenoid estimate
text: The same general min-max machinery can be applied to very different geometric families. The energy bound and topological detection must be supplied anew for each application. Definition 10.1.1 (Willmore energy and normalization) . 9E90E1906976 For a smooth immersed closed surface $\Sigma \subset S^3$ in the unit round sphere, set \[  \mathcal W(\Sigma )=\int _\Sigma (1+H_{\mathrm{av}}^2)\, dA, \qquad H_{\mathrm{av}}=(k_1+k_2)/2.  \] For a surface in $\mathbb R^3$ the corresponding energy is $\int _\Sigma H_{\mathrm{av}}^2\, dA$. The subscript distinguishes averaged mean curvature from the trace convention in Definition 7.1.1 . Source: [ MNWill ] , Definition 1.2, p. 685. Theorem 10.1.2 (The Willmore bound for embedded positive-genus surfaces) . 1EB4A795BBF2 A smooth connected closed embedded surface $\Sigma \subset S^3$ of genus at least one satisfies $\mathcal W(\Sigma )\geq 2\pi ^2$. Equality holds precisely for conformal images of the Clifford torus $S^1(1/\sqrt2)\times S^1(1/\sqrt2)$. Source: [ MNWill ] , Theorem A, p. 685. The proof is external. Its main bridge constructs a canonical family controlled by the Willmore energy and uses its topology to force a min-max lower bound; it is not a consequence of the Weyl asymptotic formula. Remark 10.1.3 (What the catenoid estimate supplies) . 1D4901862AD8 For a closed two-sided unstable embedded minimal surface in a three-manifold, the first negative direction for area produces nearby sheets with a quadratic area decrease. Ketover–Marques–Neves [ KMN ] , Section 2 and Theorem 2.4, control the cost of inserting and opening connecting necks, obtaining suitable families whose areas remain strictly below twice the central area. Their logarithmic neck estimate resolves the critical two-dimensional comparison. A complete formulation of the deformation and its topology is still an external dependency here. Applications must retain the particular sweepout class; the estimate is not a general theorem that all min-max limits have multiplicity one. Theorem 10.1.4 (One-parameter width in positive Ricci curvature) . 7A5ED0EFD787 Let $(M^{n+1},g)$ be smooth, closed, connected, and orientable, with $2\leq n\leq 6$ and $\operatorname {Ric}_ g>0$. Consider the classical Almgren–Pitts width of the integral fundamental class, using one-parameter integer-cycle sweepouts based at the zero cycle. This width is realized with multiplicity one by an orientable embedded minimal hypersurface of Morse index one. Source: [ KMN ] , Theorem 1.5; proof external. This is a fixed fundamental-class width. The source's Remark 1.6 cautions that allowing periodic families in other components of the mod-two cycle space changes the problem.

title: 10.2 Low widths of the round three-sphere
search_title: Low widths of the round three-sphere
section: 10.2 Low widths of the round three-sphere
text: The unit round metric gives concrete checks on both the normalization and the possible repetitions in the volume spectrum. The following records results from the supplied 2016 thesis, without presenting them as a complete list of presently known widths. Theorem 10.2.1 (Nurser's low-width results) . EDAAB3DCB932 For the mod-two volume spectrum of the unit round three-sphere, \[  \omega _1=\omega _2=\omega _3=\omega _4=4\pi ,\qquad \omega _5=\omega _6=\omega _7=2\pi ^2,  \] \[  2\pi ^2<\omega _9<8\pi ,\qquad \omega _{13}\leq 8\pi .  \] Source: [ Nurser ] , Theorem 8, p. 17. The proof uses explicit detecting families and Lusternik–Schnirelmann arguments, and is not included here. In particular, the final inequality is an upper bound, not a determination of $\omega _{13}$. No value of $\omega _8$ is asserted in this entry. Example 10.2.2 (The latitude family) . A2692E8AF721 In $S^3\subset \mathbb R^4$, the slice $\{ x_4=t\} $ has area $4\pi (1-t^2)$ for $-1<t<1$: it is a Euclidean two-sphere of radius $\sqrt{1-t^2}$. The maximal slice has area $4\pi $, and the endpoint slices collapse to points. The boundaries of the corresponding sublevel regions form the basic one-parameter sweepout. This calculation alone supplies the maximal area, not the lower bound for $\omega _1$ or the detection of a higher cup power. See [ Nurser ] , Sections 1.3.1 and 3.1–3.2.

title: 11.1 Constant mean curvature and constrained area
search_title: Constant mean curvature and constrained area
section: 11.1 Constant mean curvature and constrained area
text:
Finite-perimeter sets retain the enclosed region as well as its boundary. This is essential for the area-minus-volume functional, and connects the BV foundations with the CMC min-max construction of Zhou–Zhu [ ZZCMC ] . Definition 11.1.1 (The area-minus-volume functional) . 858933BEFE56 For a finite-perimeter set $\Omega $ in a smooth closed $(M^{n+1},g)$ and a prescribed number $c$, define \[  \mathcal A^ c(\Omega )=P(\Omega ;M)-c\operatorname {Vol}(\Omega ).  \] On a smooth boundary $\Sigma =\partial \Omega $ we use the outward unit normal and $H=\operatorname {div}_\Sigma 
u $. A CMC hypersurface has constant scalar $H$. Prescribing $c$ and finding a critical point of $\mathcal A^ c$ is a different problem from minimizing perimeter at a fixed volume. See [ ZZCMC ] , Introduction and Section 1. Proposition 11.1.2 (The smooth CMC Euler-Lagrange equation) . DEFFDC26B8E9 For a smooth compact region $\Omega \subset M$ with smooth boundary, a variation with boundary velocity $f
u $ satisfies \[  \delta \mathcal A^ c(f
u )=\int _{\partial \Omega }(H-c)f\, dA.  \] It is critical under all smooth variations if and only if $H=c$ everywhere. Proof Proposition 7.1.2 gives the area derivative $\int Hf$. The divergence theorem applied to an extension $X$ of $f
u $ gives the volume derivative $\int _\Omega \operatorname {div}_ M X=\int _{\partial \Omega }f$. Subtract $c$ times this derivative. Every smooth $f$ extends to a variation, so vanishing for all $f$ is equivalent to $H-c=0$. $\square$ Definition 11.1.3 (Almost embedded hypersurfaces) . D37CE32A4FFA An almost embedded hypersurface is a smooth immersion whose local sheets are embedded and, when they meet, lie on one side of each other: tangential touching is allowed but transverse crossing is excluded. This is the notion used in [ ZZCMC ] , following Theorem 0.1. It is weaker than embeddedness. The multiplicity of a parametrized sheet and the density at a touching point should not be confused. Theorem 11.1.4 (Prescribed positive constant mean curvature) . BEF02630A1D3 Let $M^{n+1}$ be a smooth closed connected Riemannian manifold with $2\leq n\leq 6$. For each $c>0$ there exists a nonempty smooth closed almost embedded hypersurface with constant mean curvature $c$, in the boundary orientation of the Zhou–Zhu construction. The min-max hypersurface has sheet multiplicity one. Source: [ ZZCMC ] , Theorem 0.1 and Remark 0.2, in the supplied arXiv v2 of August 11, 2017. Proof external. The conclusion permits touching; it does not assert global embeddedness or connectedness.

title: Definition 11.1.1 (The area-minus-volume functional)
section: 11.1 Constant mean curvature and constrained area
text: Definition 11.1.1 (The area-minus-volume functional) . 858933BEFE56 For a finite-perimeter set $\Omega $ in a smooth closed $(M^{n+1},g)$ and a prescribed number $c$, define \[  \mathcal A^ c(\Omega )=P(\Omega ;M)-c\operatorname {Vol}(\Omega ).  \] On a smooth boundary $\Sigma =\partial \Omega $ we use the outward unit normal and $H=\operatorname {div}_\Sigma \nu $. A CMC hypersurface has constant scalar $H$. Prescribing $c$ and finding a critical point of $\mathcal A^ c$ is a different problem from minimizing perimeter at a fixed volume. See [ ZZCMC ] , Introduction and Section 1.

title: Proposition 11.1.2 (The smooth CMC Euler-Lagrange equation)
section: 11.1 Constant mean curvature and constrained area
text:
Proposition 11.1.2 (The smooth CMC Euler-Lagrange equation) . DEFFDC26B8E9 For a smooth compact region $\Omega \subset M$ with smooth boundary, a variation with boundary velocity $f
u $ satisfies \[  \delta \mathcal A^ c(f
u )=\int _{\partial \Omega }(H-c)f\, dA.  \] It is critical under all smooth variations if and only if $H=c$ everywhere. Proof Proposition 7.1.2 gives the area derivative $\int Hf$. The divergence theorem applied to an extension $X$ of $f
u $ gives the volume derivative $\int _\Omega \operatorname {div}_ M X=\int _{\partial \Omega }f$. Subtract $c$ times this derivative. Every smooth $f$ extends to a variation, so vanishing for all $f$ is equivalent to $H-c=0$. $\square$

title: Definition 11.1.3 (Almost embedded hypersurfaces)
section: 11.1 Constant mean curvature and constrained area
text: Definition 11.1.3 (Almost embedded hypersurfaces) . D37CE32A4FFA An almost embedded hypersurface is a smooth immersion whose local sheets are embedded and, when they meet, lie on one side of each other: tangential touching is allowed but transverse crossing is excluded. This is the notion used in [ ZZCMC ] , following Theorem 0.1. It is weaker than embeddedness. The multiplicity of a parametrized sheet and the density at a touching point should not be confused.

title: Theorem 11.1.4 (Prescribed positive constant mean curvature)
section: 11.1 Constant mean curvature and constrained area
text: Theorem 11.1.4 (Prescribed positive constant mean curvature) . BEF02630A1D3 Let $M^{n+1}$ be a smooth closed connected Riemannian manifold with $2\leq n\leq 6$. For each $c>0$ there exists a nonempty smooth closed almost embedded hypersurface with constant mean curvature $c$, in the boundary orientation of the Zhou–Zhu construction. The min-max hypersurface has sheet multiplicity one. Source: [ ZZCMC ] , Theorem 0.1 and Remark 0.2, in the supplied arXiv v2 of August 11, 2017. Proof external. The conclusion permits touching; it does not assert global embeddedness or connectedness.

title: 11.2 Constant geodesic curvature networks
text: The one-dimensional problem has a separate regularity theory. In particular, a hypersurface theorem in ambient dimensions three through seven cannot simply be applied with $n=1$. Theorem 11.2.1 (Curvature networks on a closed surface) . 1BE70B8F92FD Let $(S,g)$ be a smooth closed connected Riemannian surface and let $c>0$. There is a nontrivial integral one-varifold induced with multiplicity one by the boundary of a finite-perimeter set, and a finite set $F\subset S$, such that away from $F$ its boundary is an almost embedded curve of constant geodesic curvature $c$. At each point of $F$ the density is an integer and every tangent cone is a stationary geodesic network in the tangent plane, smooth away from the origin. Source: [ ZZNet ] , Theorem 1.1. Its proof is external. This result does not assert that the entire output is a smooth embedded closed curve.
