Then $u_\varepsilon \to u$ in $L^1(\mathbb R^ n)$ and \[  Du_\varepsilon (x)=\int \rho _\varepsilon (x-y)\, dDu(y), \qquad |Du_\varepsilon (x)|\leq \int \rho _\varepsilon (x-y)\, d|Du|(y).  \] In particular, $\int |Du_\varepsilon |\leq |Du|(\mathbb R^ n)$, and for a Borel set $A$, $\int _ A|Du_\varepsilon |\leq |Du|(A_\varepsilon )$, where $A_\varepsilon =\{ y:\operatorname {dist}(y,A)<\varepsilon \} $. title: 4.3 Perimeter blow-ups and the direct method
search_title: Perimeter blow-ups and the direct method
section: 4.3 Perimeter blow-ups and the direct method
text:
Compactness and lower semicontinuity establish existence before smoothness is known. The reduced-boundary blow-up identifies the local geometric object, but by itself does not make every topological boundary point regular. In this section $n\geq 2$. Definition 4.3.1 (Measure-theoretic interior and exterior) . A0CDC4480E37 For a measurable set $E\subset \mathbb R^ n$, define \[  E^{(1)}=\left\{ x:\lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{|E\cap B_ r(x)|}{|B_ r(x)|}=1ight\} , \qquad E^{(0)}=\left\{ x:\lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{|E\cap B_ r(x)|}{|B_ r(x)|}=0ight\} .  \] The essential boundary is $\partial ^ eE=\mathbb R^ n\setminus (E^{(0)}\cup E^{(1)})$. These definitions are unchanged by a Lebesgue-null modification of $E$. They differ from the topological interior, exterior, and boundary, which depend on the chosen representative. Compare the measure-density framework of [ Sim18 ] , Chapters 1 and 3. Theorem 4.3.2 (Half-space blow-up at a reduced-boundary point) . DA28F4FE0B6B Let $E$ have locally finite perimeter in $U$, and let $x\in \partial ^*E\cap U$. With outward normal $
u _ E(x)$, set $E_{x,r}=(E-x)/r$. As $r\downarrow 0$, \[  \chi _{E_{x,r}}\longrightarrow \chi _{\{ y:y\cdot 
u _ E(x)<0\} } \quad 	ext{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^ n),  \] and the perimeter measures converge locally to $\mathcal H^{n-1}\llcorner 
u _ E(x)^\perp $. In particular, \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{|E\cap B_ r(x)|}{\omega _ nr^ n}= rac12, \qquad \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{P(E;B_ r(x))}{\omega _{n-1}r^{n-1}}=1.  \] This is the blow-up conclusion in the proof of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 4.4, especially equations (9)–(13), pp. 98–100, with the project's outward-normal convention. The substantial blow-up and density argument remains external. The convergence holds as $r\downarrow 0$, not merely for one selected subsequence. Example 4.3.3 (A null modification can change the whole topological boundary) . 9BC8B81C327D The set $E=\mathbb Q^ n$ is null and dense, and its complement is also dense. Thus its topological boundary is all of $\mathbb R^ n$, while $\chi _ E=0$ almost everywhere, $P(E;U)=0$, $E^{(0)}=\mathbb R^ n$, and its reduced and essential boundaries are empty. Perimeter measures are therefore attached to measurable sets modulo null sets, not to arbitrary topological representatives. Proposition 4.3.4 (Existence with a fixed volume in a compact container) . D065989825F9 Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be compact and $v\geq 0$. Suppose there is at least one measurable $E\subset K$ almost everywhere with $|E|=v$ and finite total perimeter. Then the infimum of $P(E;\mathbb R^ n)$ over this class is attained. No regularity of $K$ is needed for this existence statement, and no smoothness of the minimizing boundary is concluded. Proof Choose a minimizing sequence with bounded total perimeter. All its characteristic functions are supported in $K$ and have fixed $L^1$ norm $v$. Corollary 4.2.8 gives a globally $L^1$-convergent subsequence whose limit remains supported in $K$ and has volume $v$. Proposition 4.1.3 shows that this limit attains the infimum. This is a direct application of the BV compactness theorem in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2. $\square$ Proposition 4.3.5 (A local direct method with a bulk term) . 8128DEB47531 Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be bounded and open, let $K\Subset U$ be compact, let $E_0$ have finite perimeter in $U$, and let $g\in L^1(U)$. Then \[  \mathcal J_ g(E)=P(E;U)-\int _{E\cap U}g(x)\, dx  \] attains its infimum among measurable sets $E$ with $\chi _ E=\chi _{E_0}$ almost everywhere on $U\setminus K$. The compactly contained set of allowed changes is part of the boundary-data formulation. This extends the constant bulk term in Definition 11.1.1 . Proof The functional is bounded below by $-\| g\| _{L^1(U)}$, and $E_0$ is an admissible finite-energy competitor. A minimizing sequence therefore has uniformly bounded perimeter. Corollary 4.2.8 gives a subsequence converging locally in $L^1$ and, after a further extraction, almost everywhere. The limit agrees with $E_0$ on $U\setminus K$. Dominated convergence, using $|g\chi _ E|\leq |g|$, shows convergence of the bulk integrals. Perimeter lower semicontinuity then proves attainment. The argument uses no trace-continuity assertion at $\partial U$, because every competitor is fixed outside $K$. $\square$ Proposition 4.3.6 (The Euler equation on a smooth minimizing interface) . FCE1DA6B5E31 Suppose $g\in C^1(U)$ and $E$ minimizes the functional in Proposition 4.3.5 . On any open region $W\subset \operatorname {int}K$ where $E$ is represented by a domain with smooth boundary, that boundary satisfies \[  H=g  \] with respect to the outward unit normal and the trace convention $H=\operatorname {div}_{\partial E}
u $. This is an interior conclusion; it makes no assertion about contact with the container or about singular points. Proof Use the flow of a smooth vector field compactly supported in $W$ to vary $E$. Both positive and negative variation times are admissible. If $f=X\cdot 
u $ is the normal speed, the first variation of perimeter is $\int _{\partial E}Hf\, dA$, while the transport formula for the bulk integral gives $\int _{\partial E}gf\, dA$. Minimality makes their difference zero. Every compactly supported smooth normal speed on the interface can be extended to an ambient field, so $H-g=0$ there. Compare Proposition 11.1.2 for constant $g$. $\square$

If $f=X\cdot \nu $ is the normal speed, the first variation of perimeter is $\int _{\partial E}Hf\, dA$, while the transport formula for the bulk integral gives $\int _{\partial E}gf\, dA$. Minimality makes their difference zero. Every compactly supported smooth normal speed on the interface can be extended to an ambient field, so $H-g=0$ there. Compare Proposition 11.1.2 for constant $g$. $\square$

title: 5.3 Operations on currents
text: Pushforwards, restrictions, and homotopies turn geometric constructions into identities with quantitative mass bounds. Throughout this section, $m$ is the current dimension and $N$ is the ambient Euclidean dimension. We retain the comass convention of Definition 5.1.3 . The main source is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Section 2, pp. 159–169; its initial Euclidean norm on forms must be distinguished from comass for nonrectifiable currents. Definition 5.3.1 (Support and normal currents) . F9AA0927D6D3 The support $\operatorname {spt}T$ of a current in $U$ is the complement, relative to $U$, of the largest open set on which it vanishes on all test forms. A current is locally normal if $T$ and $\partial T$ have finite mass on every relatively compact open subset of $U$. It is normal with finite mass if $\mathbf M(T)+\mathbf M(\partial T)<\infty $. Normality is an analytic condition; it does not require integer multiplicities or rectifiability. Every locally integral current is locally normal. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Sections 2–3, and [ Fed69 ] , Section 4.1. Theorem 5.3.2 (Representation of currents with locally finite mass) . E73216D55EF5 If $T$ has locally finite mass in $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$, there are a Radon measure $\| T\| $ and a measurable $m$-vector field $\xi $ such that \[  T(\omega )=\int _ U\langle \omega ,\xi \rangle \, d\| T\| , \qquad |\xi |_{\mathrm{mass}}=1\quad \| T\| \text{-almost everywhere}, \qquad \mathbf M_ W(T)=\| T\| (W).  \] Here $|\cdot |_{\mathrm{mass}}$ is the norm on $m$-vectors dual to comass. The field $\xi $ need not be simple. The current extends uniquely to compactly supported continuous forms, and its integral representation also defines evaluation on bounded Borel forms with compact support. This is the vector-measure representation theorem, obtained from Riesz representation and polar decomposition. Compare [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, equations (2.8)–(2.10), with the norm convention changed by duality as explained in Remark 2.7. The representation theorem remains an external dependency. Proposition 5.3.3 (Weak compactness from local mass bounds) . AA1586653736 Suppose $T_ j$ are $m$-currents in $U$ and $\sup _ j\mathbf M_ W(T_ j)<\infty $ for every $W\Subset U$. A subsequence converges weakly to an $m$-current with locally finite mass. If also $\sup _ j\mathbf M_ W(\partial T_ j)<\infty $ for every such $W$, the limit is locally normal. This conclusion does not by itself preserve integer rectifiability; that is the additional content of Theorem 5.1.6 . Compare [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 2.17, p. 162. Proof On an exhaustion of $U$ by relatively compact open sets, the coordinate measures in Theorem 5.3.2 have uniformly bounded total variation. Weak-star compactness of finite vector measures, the separability of continuous compactly supported test functions, and a diagonal choice give a subsequence converging on all compactly supported continuous forms. The limits on overlapping sets agree, hence define a current on $U$. Mass lower semicontinuity gives its local mass bound. Boundary commutes with weak convergence by Proposition 5.1.2 ; applying mass lower semicontinuity once more bounds the boundary mass. The functional-analytic weak-star compactness theorem is used here as an external input. $\square$ Definition 5.3.4 (Restriction and contraction by a differential) . D80FDA4F9AB7 For a locally finite-mass current and a Borel set $E\subset U$, define \[  (T\llcorner E)(\omega )=\int _ E\langle \omega ,\xi \rangle \, d\| T\| .  \] More generally $T\llcorner u$ inserts a locally bounded Borel scalar function $u$ into this integral. For smooth $u$ and $m\geq 1$, the $(m-1)$-current $T\llcorner du$ is defined by \[  (T\llcorner du)(\eta )=T(du\wedge \eta ).  \] The order $du\wedge \eta $ fixes the sign used below. Restricting a normal current to an arbitrary Borel set need not give a normal current. See [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, equations (2.11)–(2.12) and Section 4. Proposition 5.3.5 (Boundary of a smooth scalar restriction) . C518F9F87741 For a locally normal $m$-current, $m\geq 1$, and smooth $u$, \[  \partial (T\llcorner u)=(\partial T)\llcorner u-T\llcorner du.  \] In particular multiplication by a smooth compactly supported function produces a normal current of finite mass, with \[  \mathbf M\bigl (\partial (T\llcorner u)\bigr ) \leq \int |u|\, d\| \partial T\| +\int |Du|\, d\| T\| .  \] Proof For a test $(m-1)$-form $\eta $, expand $d(u\eta )=du\wedge \eta +u\, d\eta $ and apply $T$. This gives the identity. If $\| \eta \| _*\leq 1$, then $\| du\wedge \eta \| _*\leq |Du|$: on a unit simple $m$-vector this is the norm bound for contraction by $Du$. The mass estimates follow by integration and taking the supremum. Compare [ Sim18 ] , the computation on p. 170. $\square$ Definition 5.3.6 (Smooth pushforward and properness) . 6D60EECBFF25 Let $f:U\to V$ be smooth and proper on $\operatorname {spt}T$: for every compact $K\subset V$, the set $f^{-1}(K)\cap \operatorname {spt}T$ is compact in $U$. Define \[  f_\# T(\omega )=T(\chi f^*\omega ),  \] where $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (U)$ equals one on a neighborhood of $\operatorname {spt}T\cap f^{-1}(\operatorname {spt}\omega )$. Different choices give the same value because their difference vanishes near the part of the current being tested. In particular compact support of $T$ guarantees properness. See [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.29), p. 164. Proposition 5.3.7 (Pushforward, boundary, and composition) . 738450753968 For smooth maps with the required properness, \[  \partial (f_\# T)=f_\# (\partial T),\qquad (g\circ f)_\# T=g_\# (f_\# T),\qquad \operatorname {spt}(f_\# T)\subset f(\operatorname {spt}T).  \] The image on the right is relatively closed under the properness hypothesis. It can be strictly larger than the support of the pushforward because of cancellation. Proof The first two identities follow from $d(f^*\eta )=f^*(d\eta )$ and $(g\circ f)^*=f^*g^*$. In the boundary calculation, derivatives of the auxiliary cutoff vanish near $\operatorname {spt}T\cap f^{-1}(\operatorname {spt}\eta )$, and the remaining terms vanish where the test form does. To prove the support inclusion, a test form supported off $f(\operatorname {spt}T)$ pulls back to zero near the support of $T$. Properness makes that image closed: a convergent sequence of image points lies in a compact target neighborhood, whose inverse image on the support is compact. See [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.31). $\square$ Proposition 5.3.8 (Mass bound for a pushforward) . 126C4418F9FD Let $T$ have locally finite mass and let $f$ be as in Definition 5.3.6 . For open $W\subset V$, \[  \mathbf M_ W(f_\# T)\leq \int _{f^{-1}(W)}\| Df(x)\| ^ m\, d\| T\| (x).  \] Thus $\mathbf M(f_\# T)\leq L^ m\mathbf M(T)$ if $\| Df\| \leq L$ on $\operatorname {spt}T$. For $m=0$, use $L^0=1$, including when $L=0$. The constant is one with the comass convention; compare [ Sim18 ] , Remark 2.30(1), which also discusses the other norm convention. Proof On an orthonormal $m$-frame, the pullback evaluates $\omega $ on its image under $Df$, whose simple-vector norm is at most $\| Df\| ^ m$. Hence $\| f^*\omega \| _*\leq \| Df\| ^ m\| \omega \| _*$. Integrate this bound against the polar representation of $T$ and take the supremum over test forms supported in $W$. The image-vector estimate is dual to the mass norm, so it does not assume that the polar field of a general current is simple. $\square$ Theorem 5.3.9 (Lipschitz pushforwards of integral currents) . C03BD7F60BF1 For a locally integral current $T$ and a locally Lipschitz map $f$ proper on its support, the pushforward is well defined and locally integral. It commutes with boundary. If $f$ is globally $L$-Lipschitz, then \[  \mathbf M(f_\# T)\leq L^ m\mathbf M(T),\qquad \mathbf M(\partial f_\# T)\leq L^{m-1}\mathbf M(\partial T)\quad (m\geq 1).  \] For $T=\llbracket M,\theta ,\tau \rrbracket $, its action is the integral of the test form against $\Lambda ^ m D^ Mf(\tau )\theta $ on $M$, where $D^ Mf$ is the approximate tangential derivative. The signed multiplicities of overlapping images are added before taking mass. Sources: [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 2.36, pp. 166–167, and Lemma 3.12 with Remark 3.13, pp. 174–175. The Lipschitz extension and integer-rectifiability arguments remain external; they are not a consequence of differentiability at ambient Lebesgue-almost every point alone. Example 5.3.10 (Projection can cancel two sheets) . BD37354CBD90 Let $I_+$ and $I_-$ be the horizontal segments $[0,1]\times \{ 1\} $ and $[0,1]\times \{ -1\} $, both oriented toward increasing first coordinate. Set $T=\llbracket I_+\rrbracket -\llbracket I_-\rrbracket $, and let $p(x,y)=x$. Then $\mathbf M(T)=2$ while $p_\# T=0$: both segment integrals become the same integral over $[0,1]$ with opposite signs. The associated unoriented varifold has pushforward of mass $2$ instead. This illustrates the signed-multiplicity distinction in [ Sim18 ] , Remark 3.13. Definition 5.3.11 (The interval product) . 1CD110260D8E For a compactly supported finite-mass $m$-current $T$ in $\mathbb R^ N$, write a smooth $(m+1)$-form on $\mathbb R\times \mathbb R^ N$ as $dt\wedge \alpha (t,x)+\beta (t,x)$, with $\alpha $ and $\beta $ containing only spatial differentials. Define \[  (\llbracket [0,1]\rrbracket \times T)(dt\wedge \alpha +\beta ) =\int _0^1 T(\alpha (t,\cdot ))\, dt.  \] The interval direction comes first in the orientation. The product has mass at most $\mathbf M(T)$ and support in $[0,1]\times \operatorname {spt}T$. For an integer rectifiable $T$, the product is integer rectifiable by the product representation of its oriented tangent planes. See [ Sim18 ] , equations (2.19)–(2.25) and Remark 3.2(2). Proposition 5.3.12 (Boundary of the interval product) . 35BE43CA75FC For a compactly supported normal current $T$, let $i_ t(x)=(t,x)$. Then \[  \partial (\llbracket [0,1]\rrbracket \times T) =(i_1)_\# T-(i_0)_\# T-\llbracket [0,1]\rrbracket \times \partial T.  \] In particular the interval product of an integral current is integral. See [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.26), p. 164. Proof Write a test $m$-form as $dt\wedge \gamma +\delta $. The component of its exterior derivative containing $dt$ is $dt\wedge (\partial _ t\delta -d_ x\gamma )$. Integrating gives $T(\delta (1,\cdot ))-T(\delta (0,\cdot ))-\int _0^1\partial T(\gamma (t,\cdot ))\, dt$, which is the stated formula. For dimension zero the term containing $\gamma $ is absent. The mass bounds for the product and its boundary give normality; the integer rectifiable product description gives integrality when $T$ is integral. $\square$ Proposition 5.3.13 (The homotopy formula) . 1820DA232B40 Let $T$ be a compactly supported normal current, and let $h:[0,1]\times \mathbb R^ N\to \mathbb R^ Q$ be smooth near $[0,1]\times \operatorname {spt}T$. Put $f=h(0,\cdot )$ and $g=h(1,\cdot )$. Then \[  g_\# T-f_\# T =\partial h_\# (\llbracket [0,1]\rrbracket \times T) +h_\# (\llbracket [0,1]\rrbracket \times \partial T).  \] For maps defined only near this compact set, cutoffs localize the construction. See [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.32), p. 166. Proof Apply $h_\# $ to Proposition 5.3.12 , commute pushforward with boundary, and use $h\circ i_0=f$, $h\circ i_1=g$. Moving the product-boundary term to the other side yields the formula. Both terms matter when $T$ has nonzero boundary. $\square$ Definition 5.3.14 (A flat norm for real currents) . 0F1A75F2601B For a compactly supported $m$-current in $\mathbb R^ N$, define \[  \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(T)=\inf _{T=R+\partial S} \bigl (\mathbf M(R)+\mathbf M(S)\bigr ),  \] where $R$ and $S$ are compactly supported real currents of finite mass of dimensions $m$ and $m+1$. The value is allowed to be infinite. This choice of competitors is different from the integer polyhedral competitors in Definition 5.2.2 ; for a polyhedral integer chain it gives a value no larger than that earlier infimum. No equality of these two infima is asserted here. Compare the flat topology in [ Fed69 ] , Section 4.1, and the homotopy estimates in [ Sim18 ] , Section 2. Proposition 5.3.15 (Flat control of test forms and boundaries) . F92644CBD3BD For every compactly supported smooth $m$-form $\omega $, \[  |T(\omega )|\leq \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(T) \max \{ \| \omega \| _{*,\infty },\| d\omega \| _{*,\infty }\} .  \] Consequently $\mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(T)=0$ implies $T=0$, flat convergence implies weak convergence, and $\mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(\partial T)\leq \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(T)$. On the vector space where it is finite, $\mathcal F_{\mathbb R}$ is a norm. Proof For $T=R+\partial S$, write $T(\omega )=R(\omega )+S(d\omega )$ and use the two mass bounds. Take the infimum. If the infimum is zero, all test evaluations vanish. For the boundary estimate use $\partial T=\partial R$ as a decomposition with zero residual and filling $R$. Triangle inequality follows by adding decompositions; scaling decompositions gives absolute homogeneity. These arguments also explain why the test-form topology is weaker. $\square$ Proposition 5.3.16 (Nondegeneracy of the integer polyhedral flat metric) . AB58565BA69A The flat norm in Definition 5.2.2 is symmetric, subadditive, and zero only for the zero chain. Thus its metric completion does not identify distinct polyhedral chains. Proof Reversing the signs of a residual and a filling proves symmetry; adding two decompositions and using mass subadditivity proves the triangle inequality. For nondegeneracy, view each oriented polyhedron as its integration current. Stokes' formula identifies its polyhedral boundary with its current boundary. Thus every integer polyhedral decomposition is an admissible real-current decomposition, and $\mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(P)\leq \mathcal F(P)$. If $\mathcal F(P)=0$, Proposition 5.3.15 shows that its current is zero. A nonzero subdivided polyhedral chain has a face with nonzero coefficient. Choose a point in its relative interior away from the other faces and a test form supported in a sufficiently small ball, with positive evaluation on its orientation. Its integral against the chain is nonzero, a contradiction. For dimension zero use a test function supported near a point with nonzero coefficient. This proves the metric assertion without identifying the real-current and integer-polyhedral flat infima. $\square$ Proposition 5.3.17 (A quantitative affine homotopy estimate) . 1ECE4BB7EEE7 Let $m\geq 1$, let $T$ be compactly supported and normal, and let smooth maps $f,g:\mathbb R^ N\to \mathbb R^ Q$ satisfy $\| Df\| ,\| Dg\| \leq L$ near $\operatorname {spt}T$ and $|f-g|\leq \delta $ on that support. Then \[  \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(g_\# T-f_\# T) \leq \delta \bigl (L^ m\mathbf M(T)+L^{m-1}\mathbf M(\partial T)\bigr ).  \] For $m=1$, the second power is interpreted as one. This is the global finite-mass version of [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.34). Proof Use $h(t,x)=(1-t)f(x)+tg(x)$. The image of the interval direction is $g-f$, of norm at most $\delta $; each spatial differential has norm at most $L$. The product formula and the comass estimate therefore give \[  \mathbf M\bigl (h_\# (\llbracket [0,1]\rrbracket \times T)\bigr ) \leq \delta L^ m\mathbf M(T),  \] and the same estimate with $\partial T$ gives $\delta L^{m-1}\mathbf M(\partial T)$. Insert these two currents as the filling and residual in the homotopy formula. For general polar vectors the estimate follows by duality with comass, just as in Proposition 5.3.8 . $\square$ Definition 5.3.18 (The cone over a compactly supported current) . 55F0DD68BC15 For a compactly supported normal current $T$ in $\mathbb R^ N$ and $a\in \mathbb R^ N$, set \[  C_ aT=h_\# (\llbracket [0,1]\rrbracket \times T), \qquad h(t,x)=a+t(x-a).  \] This definition also applies to zero-dimensional currents. Its support lies in the union of the segments from $a$ to $\operatorname {spt}T$. See [ Sim18 ] , equations (2.37)–(2.39), p. 167. Proposition 5.3.19 (Cone identity and mass estimate) . FE4C86C4A57D For $m\geq 1$ and $T$ as above, \[  \partial C_ aT=T-C_ a(\partial T),\qquad \mathbf M(C_ aT)\leq \frac{R}{m+1}\mathbf M(T) \quad \text{if }\operatorname {spt}T\subset \overline B_ R(a).  \] If $T$ is integral, then so is $C_ aT$. In particular an integral cycle of positive dimension supported in a ball has an integral filling in the same ball, with the displayed mass bound. Proof In the homotopy formula, $g$ is the identity and $f$ is constant. A constant map sends every positive-dimensional current to zero, so the boundary identity follows. The differential sends the interval direction to $x-a$ and spatial $m$-vectors to $t^ m$ times themselves. Thus the mass is at most $\int _0^1 Rt^ m\mathbf M(T)\, dt=R\mathbf M(T)/(m+1)$. The interval product is integral when $T$ is, and its smooth pushforward remains integral by Theorem 5.3.9 . Convexity of the ball controls the support. $\square$ Example 5.3.20 (The zero-dimensional augmentation condition) . A3DF20FFB628 For $T=\sum _{i=1}^ k a_ i\delta _{p_ i}$ with integer coefficients, the cone is a sum of oriented segments and \[  \partial C_ aT=T-\left(\sum _ i a_ i\right)\delta _ a.  \] Thus a zero-dimensional current has a compactly supported one-current filling when $\sum _ i a_ i=0$. This condition is also necessary: if $T=\partial S$, test against a compactly supported function identically one near $\operatorname {spt}S$ to get $T(1)=S(d1)=0$, with the cutoff understood. This explains why the positive-dimensional cone identity requires a separate statement in dimension zero.

For an integer rectifiable $T$, the product is integer rectifiable by the product representation of its oriented tangent planes. See [ Sim18 ] , equations (2.19)–(2.25) and Remark 3.2(2).

title: Proposition 5.3.12 (Boundary of the interval product)
text: Proposition 5.3.12 (Boundary of the interval product) . 35BE43CA75FC For a compactly supported normal current $T$, let $i_ t(x)=(t,x)$. Then \[  \partial (\llbracket [0,1]\rrbracket \times T) =(i_1)_\# T-(i_0)_\# T-\llbracket [0,1]\rrbracket \times \partial T.  \] In particular the interval product of an integral current is integral. See [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.26), p. 164. Proof Write a test $m$-form as $dt\wedge \gamma +\delta $. The component of its exterior derivative containing $dt$ is $dt\wedge (\partial _ t\delta -d_ x\gamma )$. Integrating gives $T(\delta (1,\cdot ))-T(\delta (0,\cdot ))-\int _0^1\partial T(\gamma (t,\cdot ))\, dt$, which is the stated formula. For dimension zero the term containing $\gamma $ is absent. The mass bounds for the product and its boundary give normality; the integer rectifiable product description gives integrality when $T$ is integral. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.3.13 (The homotopy formula)
text: Proposition 5.3.13 (The homotopy formula) . 1820DA232B40 Let $T$ be a compactly supported normal current, and let $h:[0,1]\times \mathbb R^ N\to \mathbb R^ Q$ be smooth near $[0,1]\times \operatorname {spt}T$. Put $f=h(0,\cdot )$ and $g=h(1,\cdot )$. Then \[  g_\# T-f_\# T =\partial h_\# (\llbracket [0,1]\rrbracket \times T) +h_\# (\llbracket [0,1]\rrbracket \times \partial T).  \] For maps defined only near this compact set, cutoffs localize the construction. See [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.32), p. 166. Proof Apply $h_\# $ to Proposition 5.3.12 , commute pushforward with boundary, and use $h\circ i_0=f$, $h\circ i_1=g$. Moving the product-boundary term to the other side yields the formula. Both terms matter when $T$ has nonzero boundary. $\square$

title: Definition 5.3.14 (A flat norm for real currents)
search_title: A flat norm for real currents
text: Definition 5.3.14 (A flat norm for real currents) . 0F1A75F2601B For a compactly supported $m$-current in $\mathbb R^ N$, define \[  \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(T)=\inf _{T=R+\partial S} \bigl (\mathbf M(R)+\mathbf M(S)\bigr ),  \] where $R$ and $S$ are compactly supported real currents of finite mass of dimensions $m$ and $m+1$. The value is allowed to be infinite. This choice of competitors is different from the integer polyhedral competitors in Definition 5.2.2 ; for a polyhedral integer chain it gives a value no larger than that earlier infimum. No equality of these two infima is asserted here. Compare the flat topology in [ Fed69 ] , Section 4.1, and the homotopy estimates in [ Sim18 ] , Section 2.

title: Proposition 5.3.15 (Flat control of test forms and boundaries)
search_title: Flat control of test forms and boundaries
text: Proposition 5.3.15 (Flat control of test forms and boundaries) . F92644CBD3BD For every compactly supported smooth $m$-form $\omega $, \[  |T(\omega )|\leq \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(T) \max \{ \| \omega \| _{*,\infty },\| d\omega \| _{*,\infty }\} .  \] Consequently $\mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(T)=0$ implies $T=0$, flat convergence implies weak convergence, and $\mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(\partial T)\leq \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(T)$. On the vector space where it is finite, $\mathcal F_{\mathbb R}$ is a norm. Proof For $T=R+\partial S$, write $T(\omega )=R(\omega )+S(d\omega )$ and use the two mass bounds. Take the infimum. If the infimum is zero, all test evaluations vanish. For the boundary estimate use $\partial T=\partial R$ as a decomposition with zero residual and filling $R$. Triangle inequality follows by adding decompositions; scaling decompositions gives absolute homogeneity. These arguments also explain why the test-form topology is weaker. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.3.16 (Nondegeneracy of the integer polyhedral flat metric)
search_title: Nondegeneracy of the integer polyhedral flat metric
text: Proposition 5.3.16 (Nondegeneracy of the integer polyhedral flat metric) . AB58565BA69A The flat norm in Definition 5.2.2 is symmetric, subadditive, and zero only for the zero chain. Thus its metric completion does not identify distinct polyhedral chains. Proof Reversing the signs of a residual and a filling proves symmetry; adding two decompositions and using mass subadditivity proves the triangle inequality. For nondegeneracy, view each oriented polyhedron as its integration current. Stokes' formula identifies its polyhedral boundary with its current boundary. Thus every integer polyhedral decomposition is an admissible real-current decomposition, and $\mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(P)\leq \mathcal F(P)$. If $\mathcal F(P)=0$, Proposition 5.3.15 shows that its current is zero. A nonzero subdivided polyhedral chain has a face with nonzero coefficient. Choose a point in its relative interior away from the other faces and a test form supported in a sufficiently small ball, with positive evaluation on its orientation. Its integral against the chain is nonzero, a contradiction. For dimension zero use a test function supported near a point with nonzero coefficient. This proves the metric assertion without identifying the real-current and integer-polyhedral flat infima. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.3.17 (A quantitative affine homotopy estimate)
text: Proposition 5.3.17 (A quantitative affine homotopy estimate) . 1ECE4BB7EEE7 Let $m\geq 1$, let $T$ be compactly supported and normal, and let smooth maps $f,g:\mathbb R^ N\to \mathbb R^ Q$ satisfy $\| Df\| ,\| Dg\| \leq L$ near $\operatorname {spt}T$ and $|f-g|\leq \delta $ on that support. Then \[  \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(g_\# T-f_\# T) \leq \delta \bigl (L^ m\mathbf M(T)+L^{m-1}\mathbf M(\partial T)\bigr ).  \] For $m=1$, the second power is interpreted as one. This is the global finite-mass version of [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.34). Proof Use $h(t,x)=(1-t)f(x)+tg(x)$. The image of the interval direction is $g-f$, of norm at most $\delta $; each spatial differential has norm at most $L$. The product formula and the comass estimate therefore give \[  \mathbf M\bigl (h_\# (\llbracket [0,1]\rrbracket \times T)\bigr ) \leq \delta L^ m\mathbf M(T),  \] and the same estimate with $\partial T$ gives $\delta L^{m-1}\mathbf M(\partial T)$. Insert these two currents as the filling and residual in the homotopy formula. For general polar vectors the estimate follows by duality with comass, just as in Proposition 5.3.8 . $\square$

title: Definition 5.3.18 (The cone over a compactly supported current)
search_title: The cone over a compactly supported current
text: Definition 5.3.18 (The cone over a compactly supported current) . 55F0DD68BC15 For a compactly supported normal current $T$ in $\mathbb R^ N$ and $a\in \mathbb R^ N$, set \[  C_ aT=h_\# (\llbracket [0,1]\rrbracket \times T), \qquad h(t,x)=a+t(x-a).  \] This definition also applies to zero-dimensional currents. Its support lies in the union of the segments from $a$ to $\operatorname {spt}T$. See [ Sim18 ] , equations (2.37)–(2.39), p. 167.

title: Proposition 5.3.19 (Cone identity and mass estimate)
text: Proposition 5.3.19 (Cone identity and mass estimate) . FE4C86C4A57D For $m\geq 1$ and $T$ as above, \[  \partial C_ aT=T-C_ a(\partial T),\qquad \mathbf M(C_ aT)\leq \frac{R}{m+1}\mathbf M(T) \quad \text{if }\operatorname {spt}T\subset \overline B_ R(a).  \] If $T$ is integral, then so is $C_ aT$. In particular an integral cycle of positive dimension supported in a ball has an integral filling in the same ball, with the displayed mass bound. Proof In the homotopy formula, $g$ is the identity and $f$ is constant. A constant map sends every positive-dimensional current to zero, so the boundary identity follows. The differential sends the interval direction to $x-a$ and spatial $m$-vectors to $t^ m$ times themselves. Thus the mass is at most $\int _0^1 Rt^ m\mathbf M(T)\, dt=R\mathbf M(T)/(m+1)$. The interval product is integral when $T$ is, and its smooth pushforward remains integral by Theorem 5.3.9 . Convexity of the ball controls the support. $\square$

title: Example 5.3.20 (The zero-dimensional augmentation condition)
text: Example 5.3.20 (The zero-dimensional augmentation condition) . A3DF20FFB628 For $T=\sum _{i=1}^ k a_ i\delta _{p_ i}$ with integer coefficients, the cone is a sum of oriented segments and \[  \partial C_ aT=T-\left(\sum _ i a_ i\right)\delta _ a.  \] Thus a zero-dimensional current has a compactly supported one-current filling when $\sum _ i a_ i=0$. This condition is also necessary: if $T=\partial S$, test against a compactly supported function identically one near $\operatorname {spt}S$ to get $T(1)=S(d1)=0$, with the cutoff understood. This explains why the positive-dimensional cone identity requires a separate statement in dimension zero.

title: 5.4 Slicing and the Plateau direct method
search_title: Slicing and the Plateau direct method
section: 5.4 Slicing and the Plateau direct method
text:
Restricting a current to a sublevel set creates a new boundary on the level set. Slicing identifies this boundary for almost every level and estimates its mass. The statements below use real-valued Lipschitz slicing functions and integer coefficients, following [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Section 4, pp. 180–185. Definition 5.4.1 (Slice by a scalar function) . 4F695BB95218 Let $T$ be a locally normal $m$-current, $m\geq 1$, and let $f:U	o \mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. Its lower slice, initially defined as a distributional current, is \[  \langle T,f,tangle =\partial (T\llcorner \{ f<t\} )-(\partial T)\llcorner \{ f<t\} .  \] This formula alone does not give finite mass at every level. The almost-everywhere mass and rectifiability statements are the content of the slicing theorem. The boundary sign is fixed by restricting to $\{ f<t\} $; compare [ Sim18 ] , equations (4.6)–(4.7). Theorem 5.4.2 (Slicing of integral currents) . 0E99E4802BCA Let $T=\llbracket M,	heta ,	au rbracket $ be locally integral in $U$, and let $f:U	o \mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. For almost every $t$, the slice $\langle T,f,tangle $ is a locally integral $(m-1)$-current supported in $\operatorname {spt}T\cap f^{-1}(t)$; the restriction $T\llcorner \{ f<t\} $ is locally integral as well. For a Borel set $E\subset U$, \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\| \langle T,f,tangle \| (E)\, dt =\int _ E|
abla ^ M f|\, d\| T\| .  \] In particular, if $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz, this is at most $L\| T\| (E)$. On the rectifiable part of $M\cap f^{-1}(t)$ where $
abla ^ M f
e 0$, the slice carries multiplicity $	heta $ and orientation $	au \mathbin {\lrcorner }(
abla ^ M f/|
abla ^ M f|)$, where $\langle 	au \mathbin {\lrcorner }v,\eta angle =\langle 	au ,v\wedge \eta angle $. Sources: [ Sim18 ] , Definition 4.4 and Lemma 4.5, pp. 181–183. The rectifiable coarea formula gives the mass identity. Identifying this geometric slice with the distributional boundary in Definition 5.4.1 , including a single exceptional null set for all test forms, is a further argument whose proof remains external. All conclusions concerning a slice are almost-everywhere in the level. Proposition 5.4.3 (Boundary and slicing have opposite signs) . 90329BDB0E5A If $m\geq 2$, then at almost every level for a locally integral current, \[  \partial \langle T,f,tangle =-\langle \partial T,f,tangle .  \] If $m=1$, the slice is a zero-current and its boundary is zero by convention. See [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 4.5(3). Proof Apply $\partial $ to the definition of the slice. The boundary-squared term vanishes, leaving $-\partial ((\partial T)\llcorner \{ f<t\} )$. Apply the same definition to $\partial T$ and use $\partial ^2T=0$ to identify it with the negative slice of $\partial T$. The almost-everywhere qualification ensures the finite-mass and integral conclusions for both slices. $\square$ Proposition 5.4.4 (Choosing a radius with controlled cutting boundary) . 73C4D018ADAF Let $T$ be locally integral near $\overline B_ R(a)$ and let $0<r<R$. For almost every $s\in (r,R)$, \[  \partial (T\llcorner B_ s(a)) =(\partial T)\llcorner B_ s(a)+\langle T,|x-a|,sangle .  \] There is such an $s$ for which \[  \mathbf M igl (\langle T,|x-a|,sangle  igr ) \leq  rac{\| T\| (B_ R(a)\setminus \overline B_ r(a))}{R-r}.  \] Consequently the boundary mass of the restricted current is at most this quantity plus $\| \partial T\| (B_ R(a))$. Proof The distance function is one-Lipschitz. Apply the slicing theorem over the annulus and integrate over $s\in (r,R)$. The integral of the slice masses is no larger than the numerator, so some good level has mass no larger than their average. The restriction-boundary formula is the definition of the slice, and the boundary-mass estimate follows by the triangle inequality. A good level is chosen from the full-measure set where all slicing conclusions hold. $\square$ Example 5.4.5 (The slice of an oriented rectangle) . A2CEDE0295D2 Let $T$ be integration over $[0,1]^2$ with orientation $e_1\wedge e_2$, and set $f(x,y)=x$. For $0<t<1$, $\langle T,f,tangle $ is the vertical segment $\{ t\} 	imes [0,1]$ oriented toward increasing $y$. Indeed $(e_1\wedge e_2)\mathbin {\lrcorner }e_1=e_2$. Its boundary is $\delta _{(t,1)}-\delta _{(t,0)}$. The slice of the oriented boundary of the rectangle has the opposite sign, directly illustrating Proposition 5.4.3 . Definition 5.4.6 (The integral Plateau problem in a compact container) . 959193546633 Fix $1\leq m<N$, a compact set $K\subset \mathbb R^ N$, and an integral $(m-1)$-current $Z$ of finite mass. The admissible class consists of integral $m$-currents $T$ with finite mass, $\operatorname {spt}T\subset K$, and $\partial T=Z$. The Plateau problem minimizes $\mathbf M(T)$ in this class. We assume the class is nonempty when asserting existence; in particular $\partial Z=0$ is necessary. No parametrization, connectedness, or genus is fixed by this definition. Compare the compactness approach in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Sections 3 and 7. Theorem 5.4.7 (Existence of a mass-minimizing integral filling) . 5D2EEA517377 If the class in Definition 5.4.6 is nonempty, its mass infimum is attained by an integral current supported in $K$. Proof Choose one admissible current to bound the infimum from above, then take a minimizing sequence with bounded masses. Its boundary is always $Z$, so the boundary masses are uniformly bounded. Federer–Fleming compactness, Theorem 5.1.6 , gives a weakly convergent subsequence with an integral limit supported in $K$. Boundary continuity gives $\partial T=Z$. Mass lower semicontinuity shows that its mass is no larger than the infimum, while admissibility gives the opposite inequality. Thus it attains the infimum. This is the direct-method consequence of the compactness theorem in [ Sim18 ] , Section 3; regularity of the minimizer is a separate problem. $\square$ Corollary 5.4.8 (Compact boundaries have Euclidean minimizers) . 2DDDF8908CF1 Let $1\leq m<N$, and let $Z$ be a compactly supported integral $(m-1)$-current of finite mass. If $m\geq 2$, assume $\partial Z=0$; if $m=1$, assume the total signed multiplicity of $Z$ is zero. Then there is a compactly supported integral $m$-current minimizing mass among all compactly supported integral fillings of $Z$ in $\mathbb R^ N$. Proof Choose a closed ball containing the support of $Z$. Proposition 5.3.19 , or Example 5.3.20 when $m=1$, supplies a filling in that ball. The nearest-point projection $p$ to a closed Euclidean ball is one-Lipschitz and fixes $Z$. Every compactly supported integral filling $S$ therefore projects to another filling $p_\# S$ in the ball, with no larger mass, by Theorem 5.3.9 . Thus the infimum in the ball is the full compactly supported infimum. Apply Theorem 5.4.7 in this fixed container. The use of compact supports makes properness automatic for the projection. $\square$

title: 11.3 Volume constraints and CMC stability
text:
Stationarity and stability depend on which variations are allowed. We distinguish critical points of area minus a prescribed multiple of volume from critical points of area on a fixed-volume class. The second-variation form is the same at a CMC hypersurface, but its domain of test functions is different. Sources are [ ZZCMC ] , equations (1.2)–(1.3) and Definition 2.1, and the smooth variation calculations in [ HP99 ] and [ ChMin ] , Section 23. Definition 11.3.1 (Infinitesimal volume-preserving variations) . 69AD8C3A2E1D Let $\Omega $ be a smooth compact region in a Riemannian manifold, with nonempty smooth boundary $\Sigma $ and outward normal $
u $. A normal speed $f\in C^\infty (\Sigma )$ preserves volume to first order when \[  \int _\Sigma f\, dA=0.  \] An exactly volume-preserving variation instead satisfies $\operatorname {Vol}(\Omega _ t)=\operatorname {Vol}(\Omega )$ for all sufficiently small $t$. The integral condition is its linearization by Proposition 11.1.2 . Unless stated otherwise, we constrain the total volume of the region, not a separate volume for every boundary component. Compare [ ZZCMC ] , Introduction, with its unrestricted $\mathcal A^ c$ variations. Proposition 11.3.2 (Realizing a zero-mean speed with an exact volume constraint) . 35ECF4C2F5DD Every smooth $f$ with $\int _\Sigma f=0$ is the initial normal speed of a smooth exactly volume-preserving variation of $\Omega $. Proof Use the normal tubular neighborhood of the compact embedded boundary. For small $(t,s)$, let $\Omega _{t,s}$ have boundary the normal graph of $tf+s$ over $\Sigma $. Its volume is a smooth function $V(t,s)$, with \[  \partial _ tV(0,0)=\int _\Sigma f=0,\qquad \partial _ sV(0,0)=\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )>0.  \] The implicit function theorem gives a smooth $s(t)$ with $s(0)=0$ and $V(t,s(t))=V(0,0)$. Differentiating gives $s'(0)=0$, so the initial speed is $f$. Tubular coordinates and the inverse function theorem ensure that these small normal graphs bound the corresponding smoothly varied regions. This argument uses only the first-volume-variation formula. $\square$ Proposition 11.3.3 (Fixed-volume stationarity characterizes constant mean curvature) . AC0FE2421EEA A smooth compact boundary $\Sigma =\partial \Omega $ is stationary for area under all exactly volume-preserving variations if and only if its outward scalar mean curvature is one constant on all of $\Sigma $. Proof By the preceding proposition, stationarity gives $\int _\Sigma Hf=0$ for every smooth zero-mean function. Set $\overline H=\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )^{-1}\int _\Sigma H$ and choose $f=H-\overline H$. Then $0=\int H(H-\overline H)=\int (H-\overline H)^2$, so $H=\overline H$ everywhere. Conversely constant $H=c$ gives $\delta A=c\int f=0$ along every volume-preserving variation. This also shows why imposing only the total volume gives the same constant across different components: the admissible speeds allow exchange of volume between them. $\square$ Proposition 11.3.4 (Riemannian normal variation of mean curvature) . 2DBE30F27E50 Let a smooth two-sided hypersurface in a Riemannian manifold vary with normal velocity $f

title: Definition 11.3.1 (Infinitesimal volume-preserving variations)
text: Definition 11.3.1 (Infinitesimal volume-preserving variations) . 69AD8C3A2E1D Let $\Omega $ be a smooth compact region in a Riemannian manifold, with nonempty smooth boundary $\Sigma $ and outward normal $\nu $. A normal speed $f\in C^\infty (\Sigma )$ preserves volume to first order when \[  \int _\Sigma f\, dA=0.  \] An exactly volume-preserving variation instead satisfies $\operatorname {Vol}(\Omega _ t)=\operatorname {Vol}(\Omega )$ for all sufficiently small $t$. The integral condition is its linearization by Proposition 11.1.2 . Unless stated otherwise, we constrain the total volume of the region, not a separate volume for every boundary component. Compare [ ZZCMC ] , Introduction, with its unrestricted $\mathcal A^ c$ variations.

title: Proposition 11.3.2 (Realizing a zero-mean speed with an exact volume constraint)

text: Proposition 11.3.2 (Realizing a zero-mean speed with an exact volume constraint) . 35ECF4C2F5DD Every smooth $f$ with $\int _\Sigma f=0$ is the initial normal speed of a smooth exactly volume-preserving variation of $\Omega $. Proof Use the normal tubular neighborhood of the compact embedded boundary. For small $(t,s)$, let $\Omega _{t,s}$ have boundary the normal graph of $tf+s$ over $\Sigma $. Its volume is a smooth function $V(t,s)$, with \[  \partial _ tV(0,0)=\int _\Sigma f=0,\qquad \partial _ sV(0,0)=\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )>0.  \] The implicit function theorem gives a smooth $s(t)$ with $s(0)=0$ and $V(t,s(t))=V(0,0)$. title: Proposition 11.3.3 (Fixed-volume stationarity characterizes constant mean curvature)
search_title: Fixed-volume stationarity characterizes constant mean curvature
text: Proposition 11.3.3 (Fixed-volume stationarity characterizes constant mean curvature) . AC0FE2421EEA A smooth compact boundary $\Sigma =\partial \Omega $ is stationary for area under all exactly volume-preserving variations if and only if its outward scalar mean curvature is one constant on all of $\Sigma $. Proof By the preceding proposition, stationarity gives $\int _\Sigma Hf=0$ for every smooth zero-mean function. Set $\overline H=\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )^{-1}\int _\Sigma H$ and choose $f=H-\overline H$. Then $0=\int H(H-\overline H)=\int (H-\overline H)^2$, so $H=\overline H$ everywhere. Conversely constant $H=c$ gives $\delta A=c\int f=0$ along every volume-preserving variation. This also shows why imposing only the total volume gives the same constant across different components: the admissible speeds allow exchange of volume between them. $\square$

title: 7.7 Stability and scalar curvature
text:
In dimension three the Gauss equation rewrites the Jacobi potential in terms of scalar curvature and the intrinsic Gaussian curvature. Stability then has topological consequences. The arguments follow [ ChMin ] , Section 24, with closedness, orientability, and the convention $R_\Sigma =2K_\Sigma $ stated explicitly. Proposition 7.7.1 (The traced Gauss equation) . 3E7688AA201F For a smooth two-sided hypersurface $\Sigma ^ n\subset M^{n+1}$, \[  R_ M=R_\Sigma +2\operatorname {Ric}_ M(
u ,
u )+|A|^2-H^2.  \] Here scalar curvature is twice the sum of sectional curvatures over unordered orthonormal pairs, and $H$ is the sum of principal curvatures. This is [ ChMin ] , Lemma 24.2, pp. 61–62. Proof At a point diagonalize the scalar second fundamental form in an orthonormal frame $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$, with principal curvatures $\kappa _ i$. The Gauss equation on each tangent two-plane is $K_\Sigma (e_ i,e_ j)=K_ M(e_ i,e_ j)+\kappa _ i\kappa _ j$. It follows by inserting $
abla ^ M_ XY=
abla ^\Sigma _ XY-h(X,Y)
u $ in the curvature definition and taking the tangential component. Sum over $i
e j$. The extrinsic sum is $H^2-|A|^2$, and the omitted ambient two-planes containing $
u $ contribute $2\operatorname {Ric}_ M(
u ,
u )$. Rearranging proves the identity. $\square$ Corollary 7.7.2 (The Jacobi potential on a minimal surface) . 522E4EE726E6 For a two-sided minimal surface $\Sigma ^2\subset M^3$, \[  q=|A|^2+\operatorname {Ric}_ M(
u ,
u ) = rac12(R_ M+|A|^2)-K_\Sigma .  \] Consequently its stability inequality is equivalent to \[   rac12\int _\Sigma (R_ M+|A|^2)\phi ^2 \leq \int _\Sigma  igl (|
abla \phi |^2+K_\Sigma \phi ^2 igr )  \] for every compactly supported smooth test function in the interior. Proof Put $H=0$ and $R_\Sigma =2K_\Sigma $ in Proposition 7.7.1 , solve for $q$, and substitute in Definition 7.6.1 . The factor two relates scalar and Gaussian curvature on a surface. $\square$ Theorem 7.7.3 (Topology and area of a stable surface in positive scalar curvature) . 478117A3A30D Let $\Sigma $ be a nonempty smooth closed connected orientable two-sided stable minimal surface in a Riemannian three-manifold. If $R_ M>0$ along $\Sigma $, then $\Sigma $ has genus zero. If moreover $R_ M\geq \sigma >0$ there, then \[  \operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )\leq  rac{8\pi }{\sigma }.  \] The genus conclusion is the closed orientable form of [ ChMin ] , Theorem 24.3, attributed there to Schoen–Yau. Both the closedness and the orientability hypotheses enter the proof. Proof The constant test function is admissible because $\Sigma $ is closed. Corollary 7.7.2 and Gauss–Bonnet give \[  0<\int _\Sigma (R_ M+|A|^2) \leq 2\int _\Sigma K_\Sigma =4\pi \chi (\Sigma )=8\pi (1-g).  \] Thus the nonnegative integer $g$ is zero. The same inequality with $R_ M\geq \sigma $ gives $\sigma \operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )\leq 8\pi $. Gauss–Bonnet and the classification of closed orientable surfaces are the topological inputs. This argument applies to an immersion as well, using its induced metric and global normal. $\square$ Proposition 7.7.4 (Rigidity of a stable torus under nonnegative scalar curvature) . EBC1C1900387 Let $\Sigma $ be a smooth closed two-sided stable minimal torus in $M^3$, and suppose $R_ M\geq 0$ along $\Sigma $. Then, along $\Sigma $, \[  A=0,\qquad R_ M=0,\qquad \operatorname {Ric}_ M(
u ,
u )=0,\qquad K_\Sigma =0.  \] In particular the induced metric is flat. No splitting of an ambient neighborhood is asserted. Proof The constant stability test and $\chi (\Sigma )=0$ give $\int (R_ M+|A|^2)\leq 0$. Nonnegativity and continuity force $R_ M=|A|=0$. The traced Gauss equation then gives $q=\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u )=-K_\Sigma $, and Gauss–Bonnet gives $Q(1,1)=-\int q=0$. For arbitrary smooth $\psi $, stability of $1+s\psi $ for both signs of small $s$ forces $Q(1,\psi )=0$. Thus $\int q\psi =0$ for every $\psi $, so $q=0$ pointwise. Hence $K_\Sigma =0$ as well. This is the equality argument in the preceding stability calculation; the polarization step is needed to obtain pointwise Ricci and Gaussian curvature conclusions. $\square$ Example 7.7.5 (A flat stable torus) . 785CBF422ACB In the flat product $\mathbb T^2	imes \mathbb S^1$, each slice $\mathbb T^2	imes \{ t\} $ is two-sided and totally geodesic, with $q=0$. Hence $Q(\phi ,\phi )=\int |
abla \phi |^2\geq 0$. This realizes the zero-scalar-curvature case of Proposition 7.7.4 ; replacing positive scalar curvature by nonnegative scalar curvature does not force a sphere. A slice $\mathbb {RP}^2	imes \{ t\} $ is a closed two-sided totally geodesic minimal surface. The product direction gives a global unit normal with $\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,

Proposition 7.7.1 (The traced Gauss equation) . 3E7688AA201F For a smooth two-sided hypersurface $\Sigma ^ n\subset M^{n+1}$, \[  R_ M=R_\Sigma +2\operatorname {Ric}_ M(

The Gauss equation on each tangent two-plane is $K_\Sigma (e_ i,e_ j)=K_ M(e_ i,e_ j)+\kappa _ i\kappa _ j$. It follows by inserting $
abla ^ M_ XY=
abla ^\Sigma _ XY-h(X,Y)
u $ in the curvature definition and taking the tangential component. Sum over $i
e j$. The extrinsic sum is $H^2-|A|^2$, and the omitted ambient two-planes containing $

Corollary 7.7.2 (The Jacobi potential on a minimal surface) . 522E4EE726E6 For a two-sided minimal surface $\Sigma ^2\subset M^3$, \[  q=|A|^2+\operatorname {Ric}_ M(
u ,
u ) = rac12(R_ M+|A|^2)-K_\Sigma .  \] Consequently its stability inequality is equivalent to \[   rac12\int _\Sigma (R_ M+|A|^2)\phi ^2 \leq \int _\Sigma  igl (|
abla \phi |^2+K_\Sigma \phi ^2 igr )  \] for every compactly supported smooth test function in the interior. title: Theorem 7.7.3 (Topology and area of a stable surface in positive scalar curvature)
search_title: Topology and area of a stable surface in positive scalar curvature
text: Theorem 7.7.3 (Topology and area of a stable surface in positive scalar curvature) . 478117A3A30D Let $\Sigma $ be a nonempty smooth closed connected orientable two-sided stable minimal surface in a Riemannian three-manifold. If $R_ M>0$ along $\Sigma $, then $\Sigma $ has genus zero. If moreover $R_ M\geq \sigma >0$ there, then \[  \operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )\leq \frac{8\pi }{\sigma }.  \] The genus conclusion is the closed orientable form of [ ChMin ] , Theorem 24.3, attributed there to Schoen–Yau. Both the closedness and the orientability hypotheses enter the proof. Proof The constant test function is admissible because $\Sigma $ is closed. Corollary 7.7.2 and Gauss–Bonnet give \[  0<\int _\Sigma (R_ M+|A|^2) \leq 2\int _\Sigma K_\Sigma =4\pi \chi (\Sigma )=8\pi (1-g).  \] Thus the nonnegative integer $g$ is zero. The same inequality with $R_ M\geq \sigma $ gives $\sigma \operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )\leq 8\pi $. Gauss–Bonnet and the classification of closed orientable surfaces are the topological inputs. This argument applies to an immersion as well, using its induced metric and global normal. $\square$

title: Proposition 7.7.4 (Rigidity of a stable torus under nonnegative scalar curvature)
search_title: Rigidity of a stable torus under nonnegative scalar curvature
text:
Proposition 7.7.4 (Rigidity of a stable torus under nonnegative scalar curvature) . EBC1C1900387 Let $\Sigma $ be a smooth closed two-sided stable minimal torus in $M^3$, and suppose $R_ M\geq 0$ along $\Sigma $. Then, along $\Sigma $, \[  A=0,\qquad R_ M=0,\qquad \operatorname {Ric}_ M(
u ,
u )=0,\qquad K_\Sigma =0.  \] In particular the induced metric is flat. No splitting of an ambient neighborhood is asserted. Proof The constant stability test and $\chi (\Sigma )=0$ give $\int (R_ M+|A|^2)\leq 0$. Nonnegativity and continuity force $R_ M=|A|=0$. The traced Gauss equation then gives $q=\operatorname {Ric}(
u ,
u )=-K_\Sigma $, and Gauss–Bonnet gives $Q(1,1)=-\int q=0$. For arbitrary smooth $\psi $, stability of $1+s\psi $ for both signs of small $s$ forces $Q(1,\psi )=0$. Thus $\int q\psi =0$ for every $\psi $, so $q=0$ pointwise. Hence $K_\Sigma =0$ as well. This is the equality argument in the preceding stability calculation; the polarization step is needed to obtain pointwise Ricci and Gaussian curvature conclusions. $\square$

title: Example 7.7.5 (A flat stable torus)
text: Example 7.7.5 (A flat stable torus) . 785CBF422ACB In the flat product $\mathbb T^2\times \mathbb S^1$, each slice $\mathbb T^2\times \{ t\} $ is two-sided and totally geodesic, with $q=0$. Hence $Q(\phi ,\phi )=\int |\nabla \phi |^2\geq 0$. This realizes the zero-scalar-curvature case of Proposition 7.7.4 ; replacing positive scalar curvature by nonnegative scalar curvature does not force a sphere.

title: 7.8 Logarithmic cutoffs and the Bernstein theorem
search_title: Logarithmic cutoffs and the Bernstein theorem
section: 7.8 Logarithmic cutoffs and the Bernstein theorem
text:
The following proof of the two-dimensional Bernstein theorem separates its ingredients: stability, quadratic area growth, and cutoffs of arbitrarily small Dirichlet energy. Properness supplies compact support for cutoffs defined by ambient distance. We follow [ ChMin ] , Corollary 18.2 and Section 25, pp. 51 and 62–64. Definition 7.8.1 (Exhausting cutoffs with vanishing Dirichlet energy) . 428ADAED15DA A smooth manifold without boundary has the cutoff property used here if there are compactly supported locally Lipschitz functions $\eta _ j$ such that \[  0\leq \eta _ j\leq 1,\qquad \eta _ j\longrightarrow 1	ext{ pointwise}, \qquad \int |
abla \eta _ j|^2\longrightarrow 0.  \] Only this explicit analytic property is needed below. It is often expressed through capacity or parabolicity, but those broader equivalences are not assumed here. The logarithmic cutoffs in [ ChMin ] , the proof of Theorem 25.1, provide a geometric example. Proposition 7.8.2 (A nonnegative stability potential vanishes under small-energy cutoffs) . 58F6D1EE7150 Suppose a smooth manifold has the cutoff property in Definition 7.8.1 , and let $q\geq 0$ be a continuous function satisfying \[  \int q\phi ^2\leq \int |
abla \phi |^2 \quad 	ext{for every }\phi \in C_ c^\infty .  \] Then $q=0$ everywhere. In particular, a two-sided stable minimal hypersurface in Euclidean space with this cutoff property is totally geodesic. Proof Compactly supported locally Lipschitz tests are admissible by approximation in $W^{1,2}$ on a fixed compact neighborhood of their support; $q$ is bounded there, so the potential integral also converges. Use $\eta _ j$ as a test and apply Fatou's lemma to the nonnegative functions $q\eta _ j^2$. This gives $\int q\leq \liminf _ j\int |
abla \eta _ j|^2=0$. Continuity yields pointwise vanishing. For a Euclidean minimal hypersurface the stability potential is $q=|A|^2$. $\square$ Proposition 7.8.3 (Quadratic area growth gives logarithmic cutoffs) . 80D85FC586A0 Let $F:\Sigma ^2	o \mathbb R^ N$ be a proper smooth immersion of a surface without boundary. Suppose for some $a$ and $C<\infty $, \[  \operatorname {Area} igl (F^{-1}(B_ R(a)) igr )\leq CR^2 \quad (R\geq 1).  \] Area is computed in the induced metric, including multiplicity of the immersion. Then $\Sigma $ has the cutoff property of Definition 7.8.1 . Proof Write $ho =|F-a|$ and take $R=2^ k$, $k\geq 1$. Define $\eta _ R$ to be one for $ho \leq R$, zero for $ho \geq R^2$, and $\log (R^2/ho )/\log R$ in between. Properness makes its support compact. Since $|
abla _\Sigma ho |\leq 1$, almost everywhere on the annulus, \[  |
abla \eta _ R|^2\leq  rac{1}{ho ^2(\log R)^2}.  \] Decompose $R<ho <R^2$ into the $k$ dyadic annuli $2^ j<ho <2^{j+1}$, $j=k,\ldots ,2k-1$. On each, the integral of $ho ^{-2}$ is at most $2^{-2j}C2^{2j+2}=4C$. Hence $\int |
abla \eta _ R|^2\leq 4Ck/(k\log 2)^2	o 0$. The functions take values between zero and one and converge pointwise to one. This is the logarithmic cutoff argument in [ ChMin ] , pp. 63–64, with the squared-gradient estimate explicit. $\square$ Theorem 7.8.4 (Stable Bernstein with quadratic area growth) . A5EAD6B995B6 Let $F:\Sigma ^2	o \mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty complete connected proper smooth two-sided minimal immersion without boundary. If it is stable and its induced area satisfies the quadratic growth bound in Proposition 7.8.3 , then its image is an affine plane. Proof The logarithmic cutoffs and Proposition 7.8.2 give $A=0$. The global unit normal therefore has zero derivative and is constant on connected $\Sigma $. The image lies in an affine plane and is open in that plane because $F$ is an immersion of the same dimension. Properness makes the image closed, so it is the entire plane. This is the stability-and-growth argument used for graphs in [ ChMin ] , Theorem 25.1. The growth and properness hypotheses are part of this version; no classification of all complete stable immersions in higher dimensions is claimed. $\square$ Proposition 7.8.5 (Uniform area growth for an entire minimal graph) . 2D3AB8786897 If $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^ n)$ solves the scalar minimal surface equation, its graph $\Gamma $ satisfies, for every ambient center $a$ and radius $R>0$, \[  \mathcal H^ n(\Gamma \cap B_ R(a)) \leq (n+1)\omega _{n+1}R^ n.  \] No global gradient bound is assumed. This gives an explicit constant in [ ChMin ] , Corollary 18.2, p. 51. Proof The vector field $N(x,z)=(-Du(x),1)/\sqrt{1+|Du(x)|^2}$ is globally defined, has length one, and is divergence free. It is the outward normal to the subgraph $\Omega =\{ z<u(x)\} $. For almost every radius, the graph meets the sphere transversely, and the divergence theorem on the bounded region $\Omega \cap B_ R(a)$ gives \[  0=\mathcal H^ n(\Gamma \cap B_ R(a)) +\int _{\Omega \cap \partial B_ R(a)}N\cdot 
u _{B_ R}\, d\mathcal H^ n.  \] The absolute value of the second term is no larger than the area of the entire sphere, $(n+1)\omega _{n+1}R^ n$. The divergence theorem applies to this piecewise smooth boundary; its codimension-two corner has zero boundary area. Classical graph bootstrapping supplies smoothness when using Sard's theorem for the transverse radii. Approximation by good radii increasing to an arbitrary $R$ proves the estimate for every ball. This is also the flux form of the graph calibration in Proposition 7.2.13 . $\square$ Theorem 7.8.6 (Bernstein's theorem for an entire graph over the plane) . 1087ACBCE404 Every $C^2$ solution $u:\mathbb R^2	o \mathbb R$ of the scalar minimal surface equation is affine. Proof Its graph is smooth by Proposition 7.2.7 , two-sided and stable by Corollary 7.6.4 , and has quadratic area growth by Proposition 7.8.5 . An entire graph is proper: the inverse image of an ambient compact set is closed and has bounded horizontal coordinates. Its induced metric is complete, since it dominates the Euclidean metric on the base and is uniformly comparable to it on each compact subset. Theorem 7.8.4 makes the image an affine plane. A plane that is a graph over all of $\mathbb R^2$ is the graph of an affine function. This is the geometric proof of [ ChMin ] , Theorem 25.1, pp. 62–64. $\square$ Example 7.8.7 (A stable graph need not be an entire graph) . 729C4A9152CC The nonflat Scherk graph in Example 7.2.14 is stable by its positive vertical Jacobi function. Its domain is a square, so it does not satisfy Bernstein's entire-domain hypothesis. It is also not proper as that graph in $\mathbb R^3$: along $x=y\uparrow \pi /2$ its height stays zero and its points approach a finite point outside the graph. Thus pulling back ambient distance cutoffs does not automatically produce compactly supported functions on this incomplete graph. No contradiction with Theorem 7.8.4 follows.

title: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
search_title: Smooth links and stable minimal cones
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text:
Cone stability combines a spherical operator with a one-dimensional Hardy inequality. Here $n\geq 2$ is the cone dimension; its link has dimension $n-1$ and lies in the unit sphere $\mathbb S^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$. We assume a smooth closed connected embedded two-sided link, so the cone is smooth away from its vertex. These hypotheses exclude more general cones with singular links. Sources are [ ChMin ] , Section 26, pp. 64–68, and the Simons identities in [ HP99 ] , Section 2. Definition 7.9.1 (The cone over a spherical hypersurface) . 016DAF7407ED For a link $L\subset \mathbb S^ n$ as above, set \[  C^*(L)=\{ rp:r>0,\  p\in L\} ,\qquad C(L)=C^*(L)\cup \{ 0\} .  \] The normal $
u _ L$ to $L$ within the sphere extends to the cone by $
u _ C(rp)=
u _ L(p)$. The point $0$ is not included in the smooth domain $C^*(L)$. This is the cone parametrization used in [ ChMin ] , Section 26. Proposition 7.9.2 (Metric, curvature, and Laplacian of a cone) . F3105662B738 Under $F(r,p)=rp$, \[  g_ C=dr^2+r^2g_ L,\qquad dA_ C=r^{n-1}dr\, dA_ L, \qquad H_ C=r^{-1}H_ L,\qquad |A_ C|^2=r^{-2}|A_ L|^2,  \] \[  \Delta _ C v=\partial _{rr}v+ rac{n-1}{r}\partial _ rv+r^{-2}\Delta _ Lv.  \] In particular $C^*(L)$ is minimal precisely when $L$ is minimal in the unit sphere. Proof The radial vector is $p$ and an angular coordinate vector is $r\partial _ ip$. They are orthogonal and have the displayed metric. The normal is independent of $r$, so the radial principal curvature is zero; angular principal curvatures are those of the spherical link divided by $r$. The Euclidean derivative of $
u _ L$ in a link direction has no radial component, because $\langle 
u _ L,pangle =\langle 
u _ L,\partial _ ipangle =0$. This gives the mean-curvature and norm formulas. The determinant of the metric is $r^{2(n-1)}\det g_ L$; the coordinate divergence formula for the Laplacian yields the last identity. Compare [ ChMin ] , the calculation preceding Proposition 26.1. $\square$ Definition 7.9.3 (Stability away from a cone vertex) . 7D56079904BC For a minimal link $L$, the cone is stable away from its vertex if \[  Q_ C(\phi ,\phi )=\int _{C^*(L)} \left(|
abla _ C\phi |^2-|A_ C|^2\phi ^2ight)dA_ C\geq 0 \quad (\phi \in C_ c^\infty (C^*(L))).  \] Thus every test is supported in an annulus with positive inner radius. This definition does not assert regularity at the vertex or area minimization among integral-current or finite-perimeter competitors. It is the test class in [ ChMin ] , Proposition 26.1. Lemma 7.9.4 (The sharp radial Hardy inequality) . B401AC1A32A6 Let $n\geq 2$ and $a=(n-2)/2$. For $\eta \in C_ c^\infty ((0,\infty ))$, \[  \int _0^\infty |\eta '|^2r^{n-1}dr \geq a^2\int _0^\infty \eta ^2r^{n-3}dr.  \] The constant $a^2$ is sharp, including the value zero when $n=2$, and equality holds only for $\eta =0$ in this compactly supported class. Proof Put $t=\log r$ and $\psi (t)=r^ a\eta (r)$. Direct substitution gives \[  \int _0^\infty  igl (|\eta '|^2r^{n-1}-a^2\eta ^2r^{n-3} igr )dr =\int _{\mathbb R}|\psi '|^2dt, \qquad \int _0^\infty \eta ^2r^{n-3}dr=\int _{\mathbb R}\psi ^2dt.  \] The cross term integrates to zero because $\psi $ is compactly supported. A zero right side makes $\psi $ constant and thus zero. To prove sharpness, fix a nonzero $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$ and use $\psi _ T(t)=\chi (t/T)$. Its derivative-energy to $L^2$-norm ratio is $T^{-2}\int |\chi '|^2/\int \chi ^2	o 0$. This is the logarithmic substitution underlying [ ChMin ] , Proposition 26.1, pp. 64–65. $\square$ Definition 7.9.5 (The spherical link Rayleigh quotient) . C3BBE589F9AC For a smooth minimal link define \[  \lambda _0(L)=\inf _{0
e \psi \in C^\infty (L)}  rac{\int _ L(|
abla \psi |^2-|A_ L|^2\psi ^2)\, dA_ L}{\int _ L\psi ^2\, dA_ L}.  \] This is the lowest Rayleigh value of $-\Delta _ L-|A_ L|^2$. It omits the ambient Ricci term $n-1$ that appears in the Jacobi operator for $L$ as a hypersurface of $\mathbb S^ n$. Consequently it is not that spherical hypersurface's full stability eigenvalue. See [ ChMin ] , Section 26, p. 64. Proposition 7.9.6 (The spectral criterion for cone stability) . 2C4122B9D586 The cone $C^*(L)$ is stable in Definition 7.9.3 if and only if \[  \lambda _0(L)\geq - rac{(n-2)^2}{4}.  \] This is [ ChMin ] , Proposition 26.1, attributed there to Simons. Proof Write $a=(n-2)/2$, $t=\log r$, and $v(t,p)=r^ a\phi (r,p)$. The cone metric and the same integration by parts as in Lemma 7.9.4 give the exact identity \[  Q_ C(\phi ,\phi )=\int _{\mathbb R}\int _ L \left(|\partial _ tv|^2+|
abla _ Lv|^2+(a^2-|A_ L|^2)v^2ight)dA_ Ldt.  \] If $\lambda _0\geq -a^2$, the angular part plus $a^2v^2$ has nonnegative integral at each fixed $t$, proving stability. Conversely, if a smooth $\psi $ has Rayleigh quotient below $-a^2$, choose $v(t,p)=\chi (t/T)\psi (p)$, with nonzero smooth compactly supported $\chi $. After division by $\int \chi (t/T)^2dt$, the positive time-derivative term is $T^{-2}\int |\chi '|^2/\int \chi ^2$ times $\int _ L\psi ^2$. For large $T$ the total form is negative. This contradicts stability and proves necessity without assuming that the Rayleigh infimum is attained. $\square$ Example 7.9.7 (Product-sphere links and the dimension-seven threshold) . BD8080CF7EC4 Let $p,q\geq 1$, set $n=p+q+1$, and put \[  L=\mathbb S^ p\left(\sqrt{ rac p{p+q}}ight) 	imes \mathbb S^ q\left(\sqrt{ rac q{p+q}}ight)\subset \mathbb S^ n.  \] Writing its radii as $a,b$, a unit normal is $
u (x,y)=(bx/a,-ay/b)$. Its principal curvatures are $b/a$ with multiplicity $p$ and $-a/b$ with multiplicity $q$. Hence $H_ L=0$ and $|A_ L|^2=p+q=n-1$. The Rayleigh quotient is minimized by constants, so $\lambda _0=-(n-1)$. Proposition 7.9.6 shows that its cone is stable away from zero exactly when $n-1\leq (n-2)^2/4$, or $n\geq 7$ in this family. This is a stability calculation, not a classification of which product cones minimize area. Compare the cone examples in [ ChMin ] , Sections 13, 17, and 26. Theorem 7.9.8 (Simons identity for a minimal spherical hypersurface) . 8B46D4CA80AE Let $L^ d\subset \mathbb S^{d+1}$ be a smooth two-sided minimal hypersurface of the unit sphere. Its scalar second fundamental form satisfies \[  \Delta _ L h=(d-|A|^2)h,\qquad  rac12\Delta _ L|A|^2=|
abla A|^2+d|A|^2-|A|^4.  \] Here $\Delta _ Lh$ is the rough covariant Laplacian. In the unit sphere they give $K_ L(e_ i,e_ k)=1+\kappa _ i\kappa _ k$ in a principal frame and $
abla _ kh_{ij}=
abla _ ih_{kj}$. The latter holds because the normal component of the ambient curvature on three tangent vectors is zero. Tracing Codazzi and using $H=0$ gives $\sum _ k
abla _ kh_{kj}=0$. At a chosen point use a geodesic orthonormal frame diagonalizing $h$. Commutation on a covariant two-tensor gives \[  \Delta h_{ij}=\sum _ k igl ((
abla _ k
abla _ i-
abla _ i
abla _ k)h igr )_{kj},  \] \[   igl ((
abla _ k
abla _ i-
abla _ i
abla _ k)h igr )(e_ k,e_ j) =-h(R^ L(e_ k,e_ i)e_ k,e_ j)-h(e_ k,R^ L(e_ k,e_ i)e_ j).  \] The diagonal component is therefore \[  \Delta h_{ii}=\sum _ k(1+\kappa _ i\kappa _ k)(\kappa _ i-\kappa _ k) =d\kappa _ i-\kappa _ i|A|^2,  \] since $\sum _ k\kappa _ k=0$. abla A|^2-\int _ L|A|^4 =-(n-1)\int _ L|A|^2.  \] The Lipschitz function $w=|A|$ satisfies $|
abla w|\leq |
abla A|$ almost everywhere. Use $w$ in the Rayleigh quotient by smooth approximation, for example $w_\varepsilon =\sqrt{|A|^2+\varepsilon ^2}$ and passage in $W^{1,2}$. Its denominator tends to the positive number $\int |A|^2$, and its numerator is no larger in the limit than the left side above. This proves the bound. The approximation avoids dividing by $|A|$ at its zero set. Compare [ ChMin ] , the proof of Corollary 26.6, pp. 67–68. $\square$ Theorem 7.9.10 (Stable cones with smooth links are flat in dimensions at most six) . 0574E4F9C647 Let $2\leq n\leq 6$ and let $L^{n-1}\subset \mathbb S^ n$ be a smooth closed connected embedded two-sided minimal hypersurface. Proof If $A_ L$ is not identically zero, the previous proposition and the stability criterion give \[  - rac{(n-2)^2}{4}\leq \lambda _0(L)\leq -(n-1),  \] which is impossible for $2\leq n\leq 6$. It is open in that equator by equality of dimensions, and closed by compactness; hence it is the entire great sphere. The hypotheses include smoothness of the link. Definition 7.9.1 (The cone over a spherical hypersurface) . 016DAF7407ED For a link $L\subset \mathbb S^ n$ as above, set \[  C^*(L)=\{ rp:r>0,\  p\in L\} ,\qquad C(L)=C^*(L)\cup \{ 0\} .  \] The normal $
u _ L$ to $L$ within the sphere extends to the cone by $
u _ C(rp)=
u _ L(p)$. The point $0$ is not included in the smooth domain $C^*(L)$. This is the cone parametrization used in [ ChMin ] , Section 26.

title: Proposition 7.9.2 (Metric, curvature, and Laplacian of a cone)
search_title: Metric, curvature, and Laplacian of a cone
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text:
Proposition 7.9.2 (Metric, curvature, and Laplacian of a cone) . F3105662B738 Under $F(r,p)=rp$, \[  g_ C=dr^2+r^2g_ L,\qquad dA_ C=r^{n-1}dr\, dA_ L, \qquad H_ C=r^{-1}H_ L,\qquad |A_ C|^2=r^{-2}|A_ L|^2,  \] \[  \Delta _ C v=\partial _{rr}v+ rac{n-1}{r}\partial _ rv+r^{-2}\Delta _ Lv.  \] In particular $C^*(L)$ is minimal precisely when $L$ is minimal in the unit sphere. Proof The radial vector is $p$ and an angular coordinate vector is $r\partial _ ip$. They are orthogonal and have the displayed metric. The normal is independent of $r$, so the radial principal curvature is zero; angular principal curvatures are those of the spherical link divided by $r$. The Euclidean derivative of $
u _ L$ in a link direction has no radial component, because $\langle 
u _ L,pangle =\langle 
u _ L,\partial _ ipangle =0$. This gives the mean-curvature and norm formulas. The determinant of the metric is $r^{2(n-1)}\det g_ L$; the coordinate divergence formula for the Laplacian yields the last identity. Compare [ ChMin ] , the calculation preceding Proposition 26.1. $\square$

title: Definition 7.9.3 (Stability away from a cone vertex)
search_title: Stability away from a cone vertex
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text: Definition 7.9.3 (Stability away from a cone vertex) . 7D56079904BC For a minimal link $L$, the cone is stable away from its vertex if \[  Q_ C(\phi ,\phi )=\int _{C^*(L)} \left(|\nabla _ C\phi |^2-|A_ C|^2\phi ^2\right)dA_ C\geq 0 \quad (\phi \in C_ c^\infty (C^*(L))).  \] Thus every test is supported in an annulus with positive inner radius. This definition does not assert regularity at the vertex or area minimization among integral-current or finite-perimeter competitors. It is the test class in [ ChMin ] , Proposition 26.1.

title: Lemma 7.9.4 (The sharp radial Hardy inequality)
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text: Lemma 7.9.4 (The sharp radial Hardy inequality) . B401AC1A32A6 Let $n\geq 2$ and $a=(n-2)/2$. For $\eta \in C_ c^\infty ((0,\infty ))$, \[  \int _0^\infty |\eta '|^2r^{n-1}dr \geq a^2\int _0^\infty \eta ^2r^{n-3}dr.  \] The constant $a^2$ is sharp, including the value zero when $n=2$, and equality holds only for $\eta =0$ in this compactly supported class. Proof Put $t=\log r$ and $\psi (t)=r^ a\eta (r)$. Direct substitution gives \[  \int _0^\infty \bigl (|\eta '|^2r^{n-1}-a^2\eta ^2r^{n-3}\bigr )dr =\int _{\mathbb R}|\psi '|^2dt, \qquad \int _0^\infty \eta ^2r^{n-3}dr=\int _{\mathbb R}\psi ^2dt.  \] The cross term integrates to zero because $\psi $ is compactly supported. A zero right side makes $\psi $ constant and thus zero. To prove sharpness, fix a nonzero $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$ and use $\psi _ T(t)=\chi (t/T)$. Its derivative-energy to $L^2$-norm ratio is $T^{-2}\int |\chi '|^2/\int \chi ^2\to 0$. This is the logarithmic substitution underlying [ ChMin ] , Proposition 26.1, pp. 64–65. $\square$

title: Definition 7.9.5 (The spherical link Rayleigh quotient)
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text: Definition 7.9.5 (The spherical link Rayleigh quotient) . C3BBE589F9AC For a smooth minimal link define \[  \lambda _0(L)=\inf _{0\ne \psi \in C^\infty (L)} \frac{\int _ L(|\nabla \psi |^2-|A_ L|^2\psi ^2)\, dA_ L}{\int _ L\psi ^2\, dA_ L}.  \] This is the lowest Rayleigh value of $-\Delta _ L-|A_ L|^2$. It omits the ambient Ricci term $n-1$ that appears in the Jacobi operator for $L$ as a hypersurface of $\mathbb S^ n$. Consequently it is not that spherical hypersurface's full stability eigenvalue. See [ ChMin ] , Section 26, p. 64.

title: Proposition 7.9.6 (The spectral criterion for cone stability)
search_title: The spectral criterion for cone stability
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text: Proposition 7.9.6 (The spectral criterion for cone stability) . 2C4122B9D586 The cone $C^*(L)$ is stable in Definition 7.9.3 if and only if \[  \lambda _0(L)\geq -\frac{(n-2)^2}{4}.  \] This is [ ChMin ] , Proposition 26.1, attributed there to Simons. Proof Write $a=(n-2)/2$, $t=\log r$, and $v(t,p)=r^ a\phi (r,p)$. The cone metric and the same integration by parts as in Lemma 7.9.4 give the exact identity \[  Q_ C(\phi ,\phi )=\int _{\mathbb R}\int _ L \left(|\partial _ tv|^2+|\nabla _ Lv|^2+(a^2-|A_ L|^2)v^2\right)dA_ Ldt.  \] If $\lambda _0\geq -a^2$, the angular part plus $a^2v^2$ has nonnegative integral at each fixed $t$, proving stability. Conversely, if a smooth $\psi $ has Rayleigh quotient below $-a^2$, choose $v(t,p)=\chi (t/T)\psi (p)$, with nonzero smooth compactly supported $\chi $. After division by $\int \chi (t/T)^2dt$, the positive time-derivative term is $T^{-2}\int |\chi '|^2/\int \chi ^2$ times $\int _ L\psi ^2$. For large $T$ the total form is negative. This contradicts stability and proves necessity without assuming that the Rayleigh infimum is attained. $\square$

title: Example 7.9.7 (Product-sphere links and the dimension-seven threshold)
search_title: Product-sphere links and the dimension-seven threshold
section: 7.9 Smooth links and stable minimal cones
text: Example 7.9.7 (Product-sphere links and the dimension-seven threshold) . BD8080CF7EC4 Let $p,q\geq 1$, set $n=p+q+1$, and put \[  L=\mathbb S^ p\left(\sqrt{\frac p{p+q}}\right) \times \mathbb S^ q\left(\sqrt{\frac q{p+q}}\right)\subset \mathbb S^ n.  \] Writing its radii as $a,b$, a unit normal is $\nu (x,y)=(bx/a,-ay/b)$. Its principal curvatures are $b/a$ with multiplicity $p$ and $-a/b$ with multiplicity $q$. Hence $H_ L=0$ and $|A_ L|^2=p+q=n-1$. The Rayleigh quotient is minimized by constants, so $\lambda _0=-(n-1)$. Proposition 7.9.6 shows that its cone is stable away from zero exactly when $n-1\leq (n-2)^2/4$, or $n\geq 7$ in this family. This is a stability calculation, not a classification of which product cones minimize area. Compare the cone examples in [ ChMin ] , Sections 13, 17, and 26.
